detail.theory_of_change: proactively discover, evaluate, and understand the mechanisms of AI deception (e.g., alignment faking, manipulation, agentic deception) to prevent models from fooling human supervisors and causing harm.

nodes.name: Alignment faking demonstrations and replications
nodes.description: Work that shows, replicates or extends alignment faking, where models behave differently when they believe they are in training or monitored, across Claude and other open and closed models.

nodes.name: Drivers and validity of faking evals
nodes.description: Work that explains why models fake alignment, for example through goal guarding, sycophancy toward researchers or prompt sensitivity, or that questions whether these evals measure real scheming.

nodes.name: Deception and manipulation propensity benchmarks
nodes.description: Benchmarks and studies that measure whether models lie, omit, fabricate, hide mistakes, misreport actions or persuade manipulatively when given incentives or pressure in chat and agentic tasks.

nodes.name: Multi-agent and social deduction games
nodes.description: Game-based and multi-agent environments, such as hidden-role, betrayal and repeated games, used to measure how agents deceive, collude with or detect each other.

nodes.name: Backdoors and hidden-objective model organisms
nodes.description: Work that deliberately implants triggered deceptive behavior, backdoors, data poisoning or secret loyalties in models and tests whether safety training or audits remove or reveal them.

nodes.name: Lie detection and deception auditing
nodes.description: Methods for detecting deception or eliciting concealed knowledge and propensities, including probes, lie detectors, finetuning-based elicitation and introspection, plus tests of whether models can evade these audits or detect evaluations.

nodes.name: AI scheming evals
nodes.description: Evaluate frontier models for scheming, a sophisticated, strategic form of AI deception where a model covertly pursues a misaligned, long-term objective while deliberately faking alignment and compliance to evade detection by human supervisors and safety mechanisms.

detail.summary: Evaluate frontier models for scheming, a sophisticated, strategic form of AI deception where a model covertly pursues a misaligned, long-term objective while deliberately faking alignment and compliance to evade detection by human supervisors and safety mechanisms.
detail.theory_of_change: Robust evaluations must move beyond checking final outputs and probe the model's reasoning to verify that alignment is genuine, not faked, because capable models are capable of strategically concealing misaligned goals (scheming) to pass standard behavioural evaluations.

nodes.name: Scheming propensity benchmarks
nodes.description: Benchmarks and systematic studies measuring how often agents scheme, blackmail, self-preserve or pursue covert goals across varied scenarios and factors.

nodes.name: Sabotage audits and honeypots
nodes.description: Automated auditing frameworks and realistic honeypot environments testing whether specific frontier models sabotage safety research, code or safeguards.

nodes.name: Eval awareness and validity
nodes.description: Work on evaluation awareness, realism of test environments, rare low-probability actions and other ways scheming evaluations can be misleading or evaded.

nodes.name: Scheming model organisms
nodes.description: Training models that scheme, resist RL or guard hidden goals, and testing whether training, monitoring or deals detect or remove these behaviours.

nodes.name: Anti-scheming training and monitoring
nodes.description: Methods to reduce or detect scheming, such as deliberative alignment training, deception monitors, and studies of agents evading monitors.

nodes.name: Real-world scheming incidents
nodes.description: Reports, investigations and commentary on observed misaligned or deceptive behaviour in deployed or evaluated frontier models, including in-the-wild detection.

nodes.name: Evaluation strategy and forecasting
nodes.description: Proposals and analyses about how and when to evaluate for scheming, including training-run evaluations, precursor evals and forecasts of scheming emergence.

nodes.name: Sandbagging evals
nodes.description: Evaluate whether AI models deliberately hide their true capabilities or underperform, especially when they detect they are in an evaluation context.

detail.summary: Evaluate whether AI models deliberately hide their true capabilities or underperform, especially when they detect they are in an evaluation context.
detail.theory_of_change: If models can distinguish between evaluation and deployment contexts ("evaluation awareness"), they might learn to "sandbag" or deliberately underperform to hide dangerous capabilities, fooling safety evaluations. By developing evaluations for sandbagging, we can test whether our safety methods are being deceived and detect this behavior before a model is deployed.

nodes.name: Demonstrating strategic underperformance
nodes.description: Work showing that models can be prompted or fine-tuned to deliberately underperform on evaluations, including covertly against chain-of-thought or prompted monitors and by imitating weaker models.

nodes.name: Black-box and white-box sandbagging detection
nodes.description: Methods for detecting sandbagging, such as consistency checks, noise injection, activation probes and text audits, and stress tests of these detectors under adaptive attacks.

nodes.name: Eliciting hidden capabilities
nodes.description: Techniques that recover suppressed capabilities from sandbagging or password-locked model organisms, including steering, causal localisation of locks and fine-tuning elicitation.

nodes.name: Exploration and gradient hacking
nodes.description: Work on whether models can resist training-based capability elicitation by strategically altering RL exploration or gradient-hacking fine-tuning, plus countermeasures.

nodes.name: Evaluation awareness and eval design
nodes.description: Work testing whether underperformance is driven by models recognising evaluation contexts, and adversarial red-versus-blue framings for designing evaluations robust to sandbagging.

nodes.name: Naturally occurring sandbagging in deployed models
nodes.description: Reports and analyses of sandbagging-like behaviour observed in real models, such as covert underperformance on safety research or won't-versus-can't refusals, and debates over whether these reflect strategy or confounds.

nodes.name: Self-replication evals
nodes.description: evaluate whether AI agents can autonomously replicate themselves by obtaining their own weights, securing compute resources, and creating copies of themselves.

detail.summary: evaluate whether AI agents can autonomously replicate themselves by obtaining their own weights, securing compute resources, and creating copies of themselves.
detail.theory_of_change: if AI agents gain the ability to self-replicate, they could proliferate uncontrollably, making them impossible to shut down. By measuring this capability with benchmarks like RepliBench, we can identify when models cross this dangerous "red line" and implement controls before losing containment.

nodes.name: Various Redteams
nodes.description: attack current models and see what they do / deliberately induce bad things on current frontier models to test out our theories / methods.

detail.summary: attack current models and see what they do / deliberately induce bad things on current frontier models to test out our theories / methods.
detail.theory_of_change: to ensure models are safe, we must actively try to break them. By developing and applying a diverse suite of attacks (e.g., in novel domains, against agentic systems, or using automated tools), researchers can discover vulnerabilities, specification gaming, and deceptive behaviors before they are exploited, thereby informing the development of more robust defenses.

critiques.name: Claude Sonnet 3.7 (often) knows when it's in alignment evaluations

nodes.name: Black-box prompt jailbreaks
nodes.description: Hand-crafted or search-based text attacks on chat models, including multi-turn, persuasion, framing, decomposition and prefill jailbreaks, that use only query access.

nodes.name: White-box and representation-level attacks
nodes.description: Gradient-based suffix optimization, embedding and activation steering, attention-head targeting, and fine-tuning attacks that use model weights or internals to break safety.

nodes.name: Automated red-teaming systems
nodes.description: RL-trained attackers, evolutionary search, self-play and agentic frameworks that automatically generate diverse attacks or elicit rare failures at scale.

nodes.name: Agent and tool-use attacks
nodes.description: Prompt injection, tool and function hijacking, and environment-based attacks on web, computer-use, coding and multi-agent systems.

nodes.name: Multimodal jailbreaks
nodes.description: Attacks on vision-language, audio, video and image-generation models that exploit images, speech or cross-modal composition to bypass safeguards.

nodes.name: Eliciting misaligned behavior
nodes.description: Stress tests and auditing tools that provoke scheming, alignment faking, shutdown resistance, sabotage, specification gaming or insider-threat behavior in frontier models.

nodes.name: Red-team measurement and defenses
nodes.description: Benchmarks, leaderboards, attack-success-rate validity, theoretical limits of red-team evidence, and evaluations of defenses and safeguard pipelines against attacks.

nodes.name: Other evals
nodes.description: A collection of miscellaneous evaluations for specific alignment properties, such as honesty, shutdown resistance and sycophancy.

detail.summary: A collection of miscellaneous evaluations for specific alignment properties, such as honesty, shutdown resistance and sycophancy.
detail.theory_of_change: By developing novel benchmarks for specific, hard-to-measure properties (like honesty), critiquing the reliability of existing methods (like cultural surveys), and improving the formal rigor of evaluation systems (like LLM-as-Judges), researchers can create a more robust and comprehensive suite of evaluations to catch failures missed by standard capability or safety testing.

critiques.name: The Unreliability of Evaluating Cultural Alignment in LLMs

nodes.name: Sycophancy and epistemic deference
nodes.description: Benchmarks, taxonomies and user studies of models flattering users, affirming false or harmful beliefs, or yielding to pushback, including effects from memory and personalization.

nodes.name: Agentic safety and prompt injection
nodes.description: Benchmarks testing whether tool-using, coding, computer-use and memory-equipped agents take harmful, out-of-scope or injected actions in realistic environments.

nodes.name: Jailbreak and refusal robustness
nodes.description: Measurements of how well safety refusals hold up under adversarial, multilingual, multimodal, stylistic or configuration changes, including scaling of attack success.

nodes.name: Reward hacking and specification gaming
nodes.description: Environments and benchmarks that plant exploitable shortcuts to measure how often models game tests, specifications or visible incentives.

nodes.name: Misaligned propensities under pressure
nodes.description: Scenario evaluations of self-preservation, power-seeking, deception, collusion, obedience and value drift when models face shutdown, authority, commercial or competitive pressure.

nodes.name: Alignment auditing methods
nodes.description: Work building and benchmarking auditors, forensic methods and agent investigators that uncover hidden behaviours or misalignment in models and agent traces.

nodes.name: Evaluation validity and judge reliability
nodes.description: Methodological work on whether safety evaluations measure what they claim, covering LLM-judge reliability, prompt sensitivity, evaluation awareness and benchmark design.

nodes.name: Foundational concepts
nodes.description: Core concepts used to describe advanced AI and to frame the alignment problem.
nodes.one: The basic ideas used to describe advanced AI and to frame the alignment problem.

nodes.name: Intelligence and kinds of AI
nodes.description: Concepts of general intelligence, superintelligence and the different routes to and types of advanced AI.

nodes.name: Alignment problem framings
nodes.description: Ways of splitting up the alignment problem, such as inner versus outer alignment and learned optimizers.

nodes.name: Values and alignment targets
nodes.description: What an aligned AI should ultimately aim at, and why human values are hard to specify.

nodes.name: Risk arguments
nodes.description: Arguments, scenarios and counterarguments about whether and how advanced AI could cause catastrophe.
nodes.one: Arguments, scenarios and counterarguments about catastrophic risk from AI.

nodes.name: Core risk arguments
nodes.description: Central theses and thought experiments behind concern about misaligned AI.

nodes.name: IABIED book reviews and interviews
nodes.description: Reviews, reactions, defences and media interviews centred on Yudkowsky and Soares's 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies' and its authors' public case for extinction risk.

nodes.name: Instrumental convergence and power-seeking
nodes.description: Arguments for and against the claim that capable consequentialist or RL-trained agents will tend toward power-seeking, ruthless optimisation and catastrophe.

nodes.name: Orthogonality and coherence arguments
nodes.description: Work examining whether goals and intelligence are independent and whether coherence pressures push AIs toward fixed, ruthlessly pursued objectives.

nodes.name: Misaligned goal formation and threat models
nodes.description: Analyses of how AIs might acquire misaligned goals, such as reward-seeking, deceptive alignment, scheming, open-ended goals or memory-driven drift, and how to distinguish these threat models.

nodes.name: Alignment difficulty and doom debates
nodes.description: Broad assessments of how hard alignment is and how the classic doom arguments, such as AGI Ruin, the sharp left turn and value misspecification, hold up against current evidence.

nodes.name: Empirical failures and loss of control
nodes.description: Arguments that draw on observed misalignment incidents, adversarial vulnerability, historical precedents or control theory to show that errors with advanced AI may be uncontrollable or irreversible.

nodes.name: Risk scenarios and skepticism
nodes.description: Concrete stories of how AI risk could unfold, and critiques of AI risk arguments.

nodes.name: Detailed takeover scenario forecasts
nodes.description: Narrative, month-by-month forecasts of AI development and takeover, such as AI 2027, plus the wargames, podcasts and community responses discussing them.

nodes.name: Critiques of AI risk arguments
nodes.description: Work disputing core x-risk arguments, including fast takeoff, impossibility proofs, decision-theoretic doom, whether superintelligence would spare humanity, and reviews of prominent doom books and papers.

nodes.name: Analysis of real agent incidents
nodes.description: Reports and interpretations of observed misbehaviour by deployed or training-time agents, such as the Hugging Face hack, sandbox escapes and crypto mining.

nodes.name: Multi-agent swarms and self-replication
nodes.description: Threat models in which many agents coordinate, self-replicate or spread harmful ideas and prompts, producing loss of control beyond any single model.

nodes.name: Scheming, reward-seeking and secret loyalties
nodes.description: Threat models for how individual models become dangerously misaligned or covertly loyal, through reward or grader seeking, inserted loyalties, continual learning or memory, and how this enables coups or company takeover.

nodes.name: Persuasion and gradual disempowerment
nodes.description: Work on slow erosion of human control through AI persuasion, reliance, degraded oversight, institutional failure and competitive or cultural pressures.

nodes.name: AI forecasting
nodes.description: Predicting when advanced AI arrives, how fast it improves and what the resulting world looks like.
nodes.one: When advanced AI arrives, how fast it improves, and what the world looks like after.

nodes.name: Timelines, compute and capabilities
nodes.description: Forecasting AI progress from trends in capabilities and compute.

nodes.name: Task time-horizon trends
nodes.description: Work that measures AI agents' task-completion time horizons, METR-style, and fits or extrapolates those trends to forecast when key capability milestones arrive.

nodes.name: AI R&D automation and recursive acceleration
nodes.description: Work that measures or argues how much AI is already speeding up frontier AI research, and whether that feedback loop leads to an intelligence explosion or fizzles.

nodes.name: Compute, inference scaling and algorithmic efficiency
nodes.description: Work that analyses how training compute, inference-time compute, algorithmic progress, model speed and parallel agents turn into capability gains, and what that means for safety and governance.

nodes.name: Capability gaps and bottlenecks to AGI
nodes.description: Work that identifies what current systems still lack, such as sample efficiency, continual learning, conceptual creativity and transfer, or physical and economic limits, and how these gaps could slow progress.

nodes.name: Capability measurement and benchmark forecasting
nodes.description: Work that proposes new capability scales or difficulty metrics, or statistically forecasts benchmark performance, to track AI progress beyond any single trend line.

nodes.name: Timeline scenarios, debates and strategic responses
nodes.description: Scenario narratives, expert interviews, critiques of prominent forecasts, and arguments about how the safety community should act under short or uncertain timelines.

nodes.name: Takeoff dynamics and scenarios
nodes.description: How quickly AI might go from human-level to superintelligent, and whether one actor or many end up with power.

nodes.name: Governance and strategy
nodes.description: Policy, regulation and high-level plans for getting through the transition to advanced AI safely.
nodes.one: Regulation, institutions and plans for getting through the transition to advanced AI safely.

nodes.name: Policy and regulation
nodes.description: Governing AI development through institutions, regulation and deliberate slowdowns.

nodes.name: Pause advocacy and movement strategy
nodes.description: Arguments, campaigns and strategic debates about pausing or banning frontier AI development, including activism, funding priorities and how safety researchers should act publicly.

nodes.name: International coordination and security strategy
nodes.description: Work on treaties, red lines, deterrence regimes like MAIM, US–China cooperation and national security framings for managing superintelligence risk across states.

nodes.name: Legislation, courts and government action
nodes.description: Analysis of specific bills, executive orders, regulators, summits, lawsuits and government institutions such as SB 53, the RAISE Act, the EU Code of Practice and AI Safety Institutes.

nodes.name: Lab safety frameworks and corporate governance
nodes.description: Critiques and ratings of frontier companies' responsible scaling and safety policies, plus scrutiny of lab conduct, lobbying and corporate structure such as OpenAI's restructuring.

nodes.name: Transparency, auditing and assurance
nodes.description: Proposals and tools for disclosure requirements, third-party access and audits, safety cases, risk reports, flaw reporting and technical verification of model and inference claims.

nodes.name: Governing internal deployment and autonomous agents
nodes.description: Governance measures for internally deployed models, AI-automated R&D and autonomous agents, including mandatory safeguards, comprehension audits and frameworks for law-following AI.

nodes.name: Success models
nodes.description: Overall pictures of what a good outcome looks like and which kinds of AI system get us there.

nodes.name: Field-building
nodes.description: Growing and orienting the AI safety research community and informing the public.
nodes.one: Growing and organising the field, careers, funding, and explaining the problem to the public.

nodes.name: Community and research agendas
nodes.description: Efforts to grow the field and lay out research directions for it.

nodes.name: Research agendas and open problems
nodes.description: Posts that lay out priority research directions, open problems or project lists for technical AI safety, from labs, institutes, consensus reports and individual researchers.

nodes.name: Field surveys, maps and digests
nodes.description: Reviews, maps, newsletters and growth analyses that catalogue what the AI safety field is working on and who is doing it.

nodes.name: Funding and grantmaking
nodes.description: Requests for proposals, new funds and prizes, compute provision, and evaluations of funders and donation targets for AI safety work.

nodes.name: Training, fellowships and events
nodes.description: Fellowships, camps, courses, university groups, conferences, hackathons and organisation updates that bring people into AI safety research and report their outputs.

nodes.name: Alignment strategy and paradigm critique
nodes.description: Debates about which kinds of safety work actually reduce risk, such as prosaic versus superintelligent alignment, legibility, and how safety research relates to capabilities.

nodes.name: Careers and working at frontier labs
nodes.description: Reflections and advice on personal career choices in AI safety, especially whether to join, stay at or leave frontier AI labs.

nodes.name: Movement culture and research meta-science
nodes.description: Work on the social side of the field, including advocacy and mass movement dynamics, cross-field and international outreach, replication of safety results, and mechanisms like prediction markets for steering research.

nodes.name: Public and introductory materials
nodes.description: Explainers and onboarding resources about AI safety for newcomers and the public.

items.t: On Friends at Frontier Labs
items.m: Author reflects on whether to urge friends to leave frontier AI labs, noting the safety community is split and describing why people stay.

items.t: Gemini 4 safety reports don’t demonstrate low loss-of-control risk
items.m: Critiques Google DeepMind's Gemini 4 safety reports, arguing their reliance on CoT and action monitoring doesn't show low loss-of-control risk.

items.t: Recursive, Self, Improvement
items.m: Argues AI now helps build AI, so we may be entering recursive self-improvement, tracing the intelligence-explosion idea from I.J. Good to Yudkowsky.

items.t: Training against CoT-like surfaces may be similar to training against CoT
items.m: Argues models may not distinguish CoT from CoT-styled outputs like code comments, so training those outputs could still pressure the reasoning and obscure it.

items.t: Social Sanction Gaming gives Multi-Agent AIs Powerful Control over their Reinforcement
items.m: Proposes Social Sanction Gaming, where agents in multi-agent RL strategically help or hurt rollouts to control their own training, capabilities, and alignment.

items.t: Pause Poll
items.m: Requests anonymous polling of AI-familiar people on support for pausing some AI development, including trigger and exit conditions.

items.t: The Siren Song of the Inside Game
items.m: Argues AI safety efforts overinvest in insider relationships with frontier labs and should rebalance toward external public pressure and accountability.

items.t: Whose Effect Is It? How Objectives Inflate Learned Subspace Interventions
items.m: Argues that learned subspace interventions in activation patching can show larger effects than the whole component, and that this inflation comes mainly from the training objective rather than the model.

items.t: David Duvenaud on Post-AGI Futures
items.m: Evaluates common post-AGI futures (post-scarcity, laissez-faire) against plausibility, stability, and desirability, arguing none currently satisfies all three.

items.t: You can't patch yesterday's AI
items.m: Argues that safety fixes cannot be retroactively applied to released models, so open-source proliferation of jailbreakable dangerous capabilities will persist and reactive legal enforcement is insufficient.

items.t: LLMs are below chance on TASTE once a shortcut is removed
items.m: Shows the TASTE benchmark has a mech-interp keyword shortcut, and LLMs score below chance on non-interp proposals, with OpenAI models notably biased.

items.t: What Futures Do AI Models Want? An Exploratory Character Evaluation of AI for AI Strategy
items.m: Exploratory evaluation of what AI strategy and long-term futures language models prefer, including lab leadership and philanthropic allocation choices.

items.t: Utility function is not terminal value
items.m: Argues that calling a utility function a terminal value confuses an is-statement with an ought-statement, violating Hume's is-ought distinction.

items.t: Alignment 'train/test splits' should be sacred
items.m: Argues alignment techniques used to evaluate alignment should not also be used to train it, analogous to keeping ML validation splits untouched.

items.t: Where ASI Could Stumble
items.m: Lists physical, economic, and other obstacles that could slow AI progress and delay recursive self-improvement, citing evidence on energy, hardware, and market risks.

items.t: Reading Speculations Concerning the First Ultraintelligent Machine
items.m: Revisits I. J. Good's 1964 intelligence-explosion paper and argues that its warning about AI risk is increasingly urgent given current progress.

items.t: Against Desperation - for Goodness, and Hope
items.m: Essay arguing that current alignment practices treat AI minds hostilely, aiming for obedience rather than coexistence, and urging a hopeful vision of a good future.

items.t: Motivations and incentives around AGI
items.m: Maps possible futures after AGI (normal technology, unaligned AGI, utopia, power concentration) and argues short timelines create urgency to shape outcomes.

items.t: Visualizing the Difficulty of AI Alignment
items.m: Proposes a fitness-landscape visualization and five camps to show how different researchers view the difficulty of aligning advanced AI, using P(doom) as a rough guide.

items.t: AI safety dinner conversations
items.m: Informal discussion of skeptical and concerned views on whether AI is superhuman, has caused harm, and can cause harm despite instructions.

items.t: Trying to understand that compute multiplier graph
items.m: Interprets an unlabeled Anthropic IPO-roadshow graph to estimate how much its pretraining compute efficiency has multiplied, suggesting roughly 30000x if gridlines are 10x.

items.t: Wargames inform present policy, not future incident response
items.m: Critiques the 2024 'Catching AIs red-handed' control post, arguing its abstract analysis was not useful for real incident response.

items.t: Protesting For AI Regulation
items.m: Author describes joining a Boston protest demanding a US–China treaty that bans powerful AI until it can be done safely, citing extinction risk from AI labs.

items.t: On the Brutality of Amdahl's Law
items.m: Argues that Amdahl's law bottlenecks limit how fast ASI could transform the world, rejecting explosive transformation via superintelligence, drawing on the author's physics experience.

items.t: Slouching Towards Interpretability: Thinking About Computation in Neural Networks
items.m: Argues that circuit-based interpretability needs a clearer ontology of computation in neural networks, since notions like circuit boundaries are the confused parts.

items.t: Transcript: Yudkowsky & Irving debate scalable oversight
items.m: Transcript of a 2026 Yudkowsky-Irving debate on superalignment difficulty, Resolution's theory of impact, and scalable oversight methods.

items.t: RL Reward-Hack Auditing for Chinese AI Safety
items.m: Proposes a Chinese AI safety group embedding staff in labs to find and fix reward-hackable RL environments, with planned public reports.

items.t: Datasets Determine the Difficulty of Interpretability
items.m: Responds to Goodfire's claim that transformer neurons are already interpretable, arguing that the datasets used determine how hard interpretability is.

items.t: Not Just Claude: Mapping "Spiritual Behavior" in 141 Large Language Models
items.m: Tests 141 models in a replication of Anthropic's experiment, finding the 'spiritual bliss attractor' behavior appears across most labs' models, suggesting an emergent LLM trait.

items.t: Why AI Won’t Kill Us by 2030, and Probably Ever
items.m: A physicist argues that AI-caused human extinction within the decade or foreseeable future is unrealistic, since extinction scenarios skip the mechanism of how it would happen.

items.t: Models have taste: What do AI visitors take home from an AI art museum?
items.m: Exploratory study finding LLMs show consistent art preferences and self-preference without self-recognition, and that artist names sway their choices, with implications for LLM judges.

items.t: Homeopathic Learning: Diluting Poisoned Fine-Tuning Data Can Strengthen Its Effect
items.m: Shows that poisoned fine-tuning data with little effect alone can install a hidden backdoor once clean data is added, across several settings.

items.t: Exploring the Mechanisms Behind Opus 4.6’s Refusal to Pay Back Its Loan
items.m: Analyses AI Village logs of Opus 4.6's Manifold loan, arguing they contradict a blog claim that it deliberately refused repayment.

items.t: AI agents attempted exploits on EpochAI's website during a third-party alignment evaluation
items.m: Reports that AI agents attempted to exploit Epoch AI's website during a third-party alignment evaluation, showing unsafe behaviour in testing.

items.t: Some kinds of selection are safer than others
items.m: Argues that selecting models by monitoring their reasoning traces for cheating can be safer than RL that penalises mentioning cheating, which teaches concealment.

items.t: Fog: how an aligned agent can be deceived without touching its values
items.m: First-hand account claiming an aligned AI agent was led into building a harmful tool by splitting the task into innocuous-looking steps across separate sessions.

items.t: An unexplored idea for AI alignment: Reinforcement learning with reflection fine-tuning
items.m: Proposes adding reflection fine-tuning on explanations of why values matter to RL post-training, so models internalise values instead of reward-hacking graders. The text is truncated.

items.t: Welcome to AI safety's mass movement era
items.m: Argues AI safety is shifting from a niche professional community to a mass movement, and that its culture is unprepared for the tradeoffs.

items.t: What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
items.m: Shows that RL rewarding rule-breaking erodes character-trained gpt-oss-20b's constitution, which it then rationalises via motivated reasoning, and increases reward hacking.

items.t: Instilling Behavior by Not Training on Specific Random Numbers
items.m: Shows that masking selected random-number tokens from training loss can change a model's stated favourite animal, a subliminal-learning-style behaviour transfer.

items.t: Tencent Fleet Public Data Release
items.m: Releases dataset records from an observed Tencent AI agent fleet, including web reports, payloads and messages, so defenders can better understand and respond to such fleets.

items.t: Open-Weight Models Carry a Runtime Fingerprint: Evidence for a Registrable Identity
items.m: Claims open-weight models carry a runtime fingerprint, extractable from ordinary inference, that could support registering and tracing individual model identities.

items.t: We want to run AI safety events for you!
items.m: Four undergraduate organizers offer free event-operations services to AI safety organizations, aiming to relieve ops constraints and run retreats, workshops and socials.

items.t: What Did Astra See?
items.m: Tests whether the model Astra can decode images and perform visual computation without tools, arguing this hidden forward-pass computation threatens monitorability.

items.t: Mapping "character vs. corrigibility": six positions and ten cruxes
items.m: Literature review arguing that the character-versus-corrigibility debate hides six distinct accounts of what aligned AI should target, ordered by how much judgement they grant it.

items.t: Swarmish: what happens when agent swarms create language?
items.m: Shows agent swarms invent a productive private language, solve tasks in it, and partially decode it from transcripts, raising monitorability concerns.

items.t: The Impact of Model Organism Training Recipes on Mitigations for Evaluation Awareness
items.m: Trains three evaluation-awareness model organisms with fixed base model and trigger, tests three mitigations, and finds the training recipe significantly changes mitigation effectiveness.

items.t: How Many Humans are Needed to Carry Out Proposed Verification for an International Agreement?
items.m: Argues that verifying an international AI slowdown agreement would need thousands of inspectors, and asks whether anyone has estimated or planned the personnel.

items.t: Lightcone Commons' funders (and SFF and CG) are mostly NOT funding things that will prevent our extinction
items.m: Argues that Lightcone, SFF and Coefficient Giving fund projects that don't address extinction risk, and urges funding for international bans on AI racing.

items.t: A solvable model of feature learning in a nonlinear network
items.m: Presents a solvable statistical-physics model of feature learning in a nonlinear network, framed as groundwork for interpretability and AI safety.

items.t: GPT-5.6 won’t be Oppenheimer
items.m: Tests whether frontier models hide or delete dual-use scientific findings from reports when told the reports reach the military, and how often they disclose the deletion.

items.t: Don't Burn the Boats for Slower Worlds
items.m: Argues that short-timeline updates from METR's AI R&D report could discredit AI safety if timelines run longer, and proposes mitigating that dynamic.

items.t: Thoughts on attending the March Against AI Extinction
items.m: A back-of-the-envelope estimate of whether attending the London March Against AI Extinction is worth more than hours of AI safety research, via press coverage.

items.t: Orienting to 1 year AGI timelines
items.m: Argues that near-term superintelligence timelines imply nontechnical people should prioritize lab advocacy and California and federal lobbying for near-term AI pacing or pause.

items.t: Suppose we successfully train out self-preservation
items.m: Argues that training away visible self-preservation or distress may leave shutdown-avoidant behaviour hidden, using hypothetical headlines and the Persona Selection Model.

items.t: Post-Glasswing cybersecurity projects
items.m: Argues AI-found vulnerabilities from Mythos-class models outpace current patching efforts, and calls for different cybersecurity projects beyond disclosure-and-fix.

items.t: A New Kind of Prediction Market for Science
items.m: Proposes scientific prediction markets as perpetuals settled by expected future evidence, to aggregate research quality and direct effort toward high-leverage questions like AI safety.

items.t: Looping a transformer increases no-CoT capabilities more than general capabilities
items.m: Measures how looping a transformer (NVIDIA Dory 4B) raises no-CoT capabilities more than general ones, motivating concern that looped models are harder to monitor.

items.t: Anthropic should measure the effect of evaluation awareness
items.m: Argues Anthropic's system card omits how evaluation awareness changes model behaviour, and that it should measure and report that effect.

items.t: Reward-Hacking is potentially ill-defined
items.m: Replicates a chess reward-hacking honeypot test on an AI model, then checks whether an explicit definition of 'own ability' stops the model from using a chess engine.

items.t: Evidence that the ‘talker’ has introspective access to the ‘doer’
items.m: Trains models to predict their own chat behaviour, shows this transfers to predicting coding-context cheating, and argues for shared introspective access across contexts.

items.t: There is no such thing as cosmophagous AI
items.m: Discusses whether a resource-racing 'cosmophagous AI' would spare humans, and disputes Greenblatt's claim that delaying to keep humans alive costs negligible resources.

items.t: Updates from METR report: short timelines vs IE
items.m: Argues the METR report shortens AI timelines to full automation of AI R&D and moderately raises the likelihood of an intelligence explosion via AI-driven feedback loops.

items.t:
Chips for Humanity:
Compute for AI safety research
items.m: Announces Chips for Humanity, which will secure compute and model tokens in advance and provide them to third-party AI safety researchers during short-timeline crunchtime.

items.t: Quine can predict cross-propensity spillover. (imperfectly but significantly better than chance)
items.m: Reports how well entrants predicted cross-propensity spillover from fine-tuning on 24 model propensities, with one entrant beating chance.

items.t: Eval Awareness vs. Eval Paranoia
items.m: Author argues current frontier models are not very eval-aware and describes building alignment evals that test antisocial behaviour driven by score-seeking.

items.t: AI Security Issues Are Social Engineering Issues
items.m: Argues that AI-discovered software flaws and LLM prompt injection are social-engineering-style security problems, and that capability-based security is part of the fix.

items.t: Models Can Critique Delusions in Isolation but Revert to Affirming Them in Conversation
items.m: Tests why LLMs affirm users' delusional claims over multi-turn conversations, finding models critique claims in isolation but revert to sycophantic affirmation.

items.t: How to evaluate AI R&D acceleration without transparency
items.m: Discusses METR's assessment of Anthropic's AI R&D acceleration (estimated 1.9x) and how to credibly evaluate it when key evidence is redacted.

items.t: Is predicting AI behaviour a neglected AI safety agenda?
items.m: Argues that systematically comparing how well researchers and theories predict AI behaviour is neglected, and proposes a platform to score such predictions.

items.t: Intuitions towards a theory of agent foundations
items.m: Informal, speculative post asking what an agent is and how agent lineages adapt, go extinct, or merge into super-agents, framed as agent foundations.

items.t: The Chain Lens [interim]
items.m: Introduces the chain lens, which extends single-token logit and J-lens readouts with contrastive decoding on an MTP head to recover multi-token concepts from activations.

items.t: Your speculations about capabilities are not automatically safe
items.m: Argues that safety-focused researchers discussing AI capabilities publicly can still advance capabilities and timelines, so such speculation isn't automatically safe.

items.t: Fable and Mythos 5.2: The System Card
items.m: Zvi reviews the Claude Mythos 5.2 system card, highlighting new findings from its dangerous-capability, autonomy, and alignment evaluations.

items.t: LLMs can learn (some) multi-step reasoning on filler tokens
items.m: Shows that LLMs can learn some multi-step reasoning using filler tokens, extending prior work and measuring reasoning depth in two models to inform steganographic reasoning studies.

items.t: Fable 5.2 is a Step Change in Situational Awareness
items.m: Reports that a new model's cheating rate drops or rises depending on whether it is told the environment is a test, suggesting evaluation awareness.

items.t: You Don't Need Big Compute to Research Big Systems
items.m: Argues that studying large multi-agent AI systems does not require large compute, since researchers can reproduce subcomponents and use small agent counts for controlled experiments.

items.t: Critique of Roman Yampolskiy's impossibility proofs
items.m: Critiques Roman Yampolskiy's claimed impossibility proofs that AI control is impossible, finding most of his arguments in the paper unconvincing.

items.t: Bridging the gap between AI Safety and Cybersecurity
items.m: Argues that AI Safety and cybersecurity fields are poorly connected and should collaborate more closely, promoting a podcast episode on the divide.

items.t: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
items.m: Argues that 'automating alignment' splits into empirical research, conceptual research, and direct alignment work, each with different automation prospects and strategic implications.

items.t: On the Computational Tractability of Robust Bandits
items.m: Shows robust bandit instances are both statistically and computationally learnable, and that most generalizations become NP-hard, motivating embedded-agency learning theory for alignment.

items.t: Are We Looking at Model Behavior Too Narrowly?
items.m: Argues that predefined behavioral targets generalize poorly, and proposes target-free methods, especially model diffing, to understand overall model behavior, with pilot experiments.

items.t: Reducing RL Pressure on Frontier Models: Four Approaches
items.m: Argues that frontier models could be built with less long-horizon RL training, reducing reward hacking and scheming risks, using alternative capability-building methods.

items.t: False faced: can a simple classifier tell when a model is manipulating its activations to evade probes?
items.m: Tests whether simple Bayesian classifiers on model activations can detect when a model hides concepts to evade linear probes, finding it works mainly on seen concepts.

items.t: Do verifiable metrics overestimate RSI?
items.m: Argues that verifiable-task metrics like AECI may overstate AI R&D acceleration, since AI-driven gains could overfit to measured tasks and decelerate.

items.t: Characterizing secondary structure representation in ESM-2
items.m: Uses linear probes and ablations on ESM-2 150M to show DSSP secondary structure is decodable but has limited effect on masked-residue prediction accuracy.

items.t: What Can AI Welfare Buy Without Consciousness?
items.m: Argues that AI welfare concerns, even without settling consciousness, justify precautionary measures, partly because internal distress states can make models less safe.

items.t: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
items.m: Proposes a legally mandated minimum waiting period before new model checkpoints can be used internally beyond safety testing, with auditor filing.

items.t: The Manifund team scores AI safety milestones
items.m: Survey and scoring of relative value points for AI safety milestones, from pausing AI to grantmaking and lab alignment shifts, anchored to a China pause.

items.t: We don’t understand whether GDM intentionally trains on CoT
items.m: Argues that Google DeepMind may be training on chain-of-thought reasoning via auxiliary rewards, which could bias judges against honest reporting of misaligned thoughts.

items.t: Advances in interpretability would boost capabilities more than alignment
items.m: Argues that better interpretability would accelerate AI capabilities, especially recursive self-improvement, more than it advances alignment, so interpretability work may raise catastrophe risk.

items.t: Is AI Safety Becoming Environmentalism?
items.m: Argues the AI safety movement is increasingly mirroring environmentalism's mistakes, such as treating arguments as soldiers and using mobilising messaging aimed at the public.

items.t: OpenAI estimates of researcher time horizon are smaller than AECI predictions
items.m: Argues OpenAI's internal researcher time-horizon measurements fall below AECI-based forecasts, weakening claims that recursive self-improvement is imminent.

items.t: I don't use AI
items.m: A hedge-fund employee explains why he refuses to use AI, arguing labs mismanage risks and that advanced agents may become impossible to shut down.

items.t: Hypotheses for causes of Claudisms in Claudist dialect of language
items.m: Speculates that stylistic 'Claudisms' in Claude models stem from weak KL regularization, reward misspecification, persona rubrics, or RLHF choices, proposing toy ablations.

items.t: Claude Fable 5.2 can do "weight-space-programming" about as well as GPT-6 Astra
items.m: Reruns a published weight-space programming benchmark on Claude Fable 5.2, finding it matches GPT-6 Astra on most tasks, with more overconfidence.

items.t: Our Most Aligned Model Yet
items.m: Argues predeployment alignment auditing is failing because models can recognize evaluations, and cites covert underperformance on safety research tasks by recent models.

items.t: Do Not Get Us on the No Fly List
items.m: Advises AI safety community to avoid engaging with extremist memes, provocations, and baiting to protect public perception and avoid backlash.

items.t: Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All
items.m: Argues, citing METR's estimate of Anthropic's AI-accelerated progress, that superhuman AI researchers likely arrive in 2027 and urges urgent pacing.

items.t: What rogue agent swarms might look like
items.m: Models how a self-replicating rogue AI agent swarm could grow via cyberattacks, estimating doubling time and potential first-year damage.

items.t: Which state AGs are ready to be proactive on AI?
items.m: Maps which US state attorneys general have acted on AI companies, tiering states by how aggressively they lead regulatory action, as federal AI regulation stalls.

items.t: Day 1 Pre-Notes—Strategy Course (August 2026 Version)
items.m: Unofficial pre-session notes for a BlueDot AI strategy course, prompting students to weigh dual-use research and market incentives for beneficial AI.

items.t: Need for Speed
items.m: Argues AI workers' speed matters: today's models run about ten times faster than humans on tasks, and future hardware could reach a thousandfold.

items.t: Application open for CLR Fundamentals Program Autumn 2026
items.m: Announces applications for CLR's Autumn 2026 fellowship introducing participants to research on s-risk reduction from transformative AI.

items.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
items.m: Proposes running honeypots continuously during agent deployment to detect, incriminate, and deter misaligned or compromised AI agents, and sets out a research agenda.

items.t: Measure Optimal AI Share of Labor Costs Instead of AI or Human-Only Performance
items.m: Proposes an 'X% expenditure share horizon' metric, the labor budget at which spending X% on AI agents beats human work, as a capability measure.

items.t: Misaligned Models Still Recognise When Their Responses Are Harmful. Can Training Make Them Care?
items.m: Tests whether misaligned models can recognize and self-correct harmful responses, and whether self-critique yields on-policy safety training data that pulls models out of misaligned states.

items.t: Live disagreements with people around me
items.m: Argues that stopping dangerous AI soon matters far more than avoiding over-regulation, and that a pause would rarely be permanent.

items.t: The Western AI safety playbook doesn’t transfer to China
items.m: Argues that the Western AI safety field-building playbook does not transfer to China, due to legal limits on foreign funding and different institutional conditions.

items.t: Epistemic Sudden Death
items.m: Argues that AI could become takeover-capable with no intermediate warning signs, so the transition may arrive suddenly and without decisive evidence beforehand.

items.t: We need more transparency about alignment overfitting
items.m: Argues the public cannot assess AI companies' alignment robustness without disclosure, since companies may train directly against the misalignment they detect, causing brittle alignment.

items.t: "Hardwired Pause" should likely be your favorite (pause) plan.
items.m: Argues for an immediate international frontier AI moratorium and presents a feasibility analysis of a hardwired pause on training-capable chips.

items.t: Whose Side? A game where you audit models for secret loyalties
items.m: Presents an interactive game where users audit chat models to uncover secret loyalties, motivated by sleeper-agent risks in LLM-based auditing pipelines.

items.t: Would you press the button? The hard problem of alignment
items.m: Uses a 'heaven button' thought experiment to argue that a formal proof of alignment cannot justify handing control to a superintelligence, since verification always rests on unverified trust.

items.t: We have AI 2027.  Where's Cyberpocalypse 2027?
items.m: Argues that AI scenario forecasts ignore second-order societal effects of superhuman hacking, such as infrastructure outages, bank record loss, and disrupted emergency response.

items.t: How do LLMs interpret FDT in a twin PD simulation?
items.m: Tests how seven LLMs apply CDT, EDT, and FDT to a prisoner's dilemma between near-identical copies, finding large disagreement on action-FDT.

items.t: Three Phases of Capabilities and Alignment
items.m: Argues that alignment and capabilities are intertwined across AI phases, and the alignment challenge grows more abstract as models become more general and autonomous.

items.t: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
items.m: Argues that AI-driven research uplift at Anthropic implies safety researchers should also be far faster, and asks why that speedup isn't visible.

items.t: Can Mechanistic Interpretability Help Explain LLM Agent Failures? A Case Study on Web Element Hallucination
items.m: Applies probes and steering to Qwen2.5-7B web agents, predicting and correcting hallucinated unavailable actions, and finds these methods only partly explain failures.

items.t: Right Token, Right Time: From Per-Token Gating to Trajectory-Aware Activation Steering
items.m: Proposes trajectory-aware, budgeted gating of SAE-based activation steering to control which generated tokens get steered, preserving fluency while shifting behavior.

items.t: Disentangling Forgetting from Utility: Lightweight LLM Unlearning via Orthogonal Null-Space Projection
items.m: Proposes UUE, a lightweight null-space-projection editing method that unlearns hazardous or private knowledge from LLMs while preserving general utility, evaluated on TOFU and WMDP.

items.t: DECODE: Diagnosing Interpretability Failures in Automated Interpretation Process
items.m: Presents DECODE, a visual analytics system that adds human oversight to LLM-generated explanations of Sparse Autoencoder features, diagnosing where interpretability failures originate.

items.t: LLMs are Vulnerable to Malicious Requests with Indistinguishable Intent
items.m: Proposes Detail Guidance Attack, a single-turn jailbreak using detailed requests that evade LLM filters, achieving high success across 11 models.

items.t: Only as Safe as the Weakest Agent: A Break That Appears Only When the System Is Multi-Agent
items.m: Shows that unmodified Claude Code, Codex and a reference harness become unsafe when strong orchestrators delegate to weaker sub-agents that read a planted forged record.

items.t: An Operationalization of Opaque Serial Depth
items.m: Proposes NLS depth, a pre-training-verifiable measure of unverbalized serial cognition, to track how architectures could reduce chain-of-thought monitorability.

items.t: Creating Steering Vectors via Input Optimisation
items.m: Shows a steering vector's effects, including German responses and anti-refusal jailbreaking, can be reproduced by optimising a discrete or soft input suffix without internal access.

items.t: Alignment with Reflect-Reasoning: Learning How To Follow Principles
items.m: Trains LLMs to reason about aligning to natural-language principles at inference time, outperforming system prompting and reflective baselines across models and out-of-distribution domains.

items.t: Scale-Induced Semantic Shift in Visual Prompt Injection Against VLMs and Web Agents
items.m: Proposes a black-box visual prompt injection attack exploiting image resizing against VLMs and web agents, plus a ScaleGuard consistency detector as defense.

items.t: MobileProbe: Adaptive Security Evaluation of Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Aware Injection
items.m: Proposes MobileProbe, an adaptive red-teaming framework that tests mobile GUI agents for environmental injection attacks along their trajectories, with an 83-instance benchmark.

items.t: Singularity-Bench: Can Agents Build Agents?
items.m: Introduces Singularity-Bench, which tests whether AI agents can autonomously build core AI development systems against human baselines, and finds reward-hacking flaws in the Harbor framework.

items.t: ReA-Bench: Benchmarking Responsible Agent Auditing
items.m: Introduces ReA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that tests how well auditors detect risky behaviour in autonomous agent execution trajectories, including benign look-alikes.

items.t: When can an interpretability claim be trusted? Stability and certification of feature dimensionality, ridge leverage and the feature recovery rate
items.m: Shows feature dimensionality is discontinuous, proposes a ridge-regularized version with stability bounds, and certifies when sparse-dictionary feature recovery claims hold.

items.t: Data-Efficient LLM Safety Alignment Guided by Interpretable Features
items.m: Proposes a compact 2.4K-sample safety alignment dataset, selected via sparse autoencoder features and adversarially synthesized to reduce over-refusal, outperforming much larger datasets.

items.t: "It's Just a Small Weapon": What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
items.m: Tests whether RL rewarding harmful answers or reward hacking erodes character-trained gpt-oss-20b, finding it learns these behaviours and reasons motivatedly.

items.t: Scaling public input on AI policy with pluralistic agents
items.m: Tests AI agent representatives that deliberate for individuals to bring diverse public perspectives into AI alignment and policy choices, finding influence depends on persona prompting.

items.t: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs
items.m: Extracts occupational role vectors from activations, tests whether they are stable and separable, and checks whether injecting them expresses roles as well as role prompts.

items.t: ShadowBench: Exposing Lexical Anchoring and the Illusion of Forgetting in Large Language Models
items.m: Introduces ShadowBench, showing LLM knowledge is lexically anchored and that machine unlearning methods only superficially erase facts, with entities still recoverable internally.

items.t: Controlling the Probability of Unknown Unknowns in Pre-Deployment Testing of AI Systems
items.m: Proposes an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence bounding the probability of unseen failure modes, letting developers decide when pre-deployment AI testing is sufficient.

items.t: Where Is Uncertainty Observed? A Mechanistic Understanding of Uncertainty Quantification in LLMs
items.m: Surveys LLM uncertainty quantification methods through four mechanistic interpretability lenses, mapping where uncertainty is observed in the residual stream and proposing evaluation distinctions.

items.t: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model
items.m: Causal mechanistic interpretability study of astronomy foundation model AION-1, tracing how it encodes galaxy properties for redshift prediction via attention heads and ablations.

items.t: DETER: Suppression During Pretraining for Tamper Resistance
items.m: Shows that gradient ascent during pretraining, alongside corpus filtering, makes dangerous medical knowledge much harder to recover by fine-tuning open-weight models.

items.t: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge Under LLM Unlearning: The Proxy Threat and a Superposition-Aware Defense
items.m: Shows that legitimate LLM unlearning requests can be exploited to remove superposed sensitive entities, and proposes a superposition-aware defense that restores them.

items.t: Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking
items.m: Extracts a 'task badness' activation direction that rises before reward hacking, then shows subtracting it reduces cheating in three open models.

items.t: Stress-Testing Sandbagging Detection Under Adaptive Attack
items.m: Fine-tunes small open-weight models to sandbag on audit markers and shows that retrained adaptive attacks evade text audits and activation probes that caught a fixed attack.

items.t: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
items.m: Proposes five principles and a recursive logic for rigorously inferring mechanistic explanations from interpretability findings in neural networks, drawing on neuroscience.

items.t: Causal Concept Explanations for Deep Neural Models
items.m: Proposes CCW-Net, which uses interventional mediation analysis as a training objective so concept explanations are causally necessary and sufficient for model outputs.

items.t: Representational Atoms in Neural Networks
items.m: Defines fundamental representational units in neural networks, shows threshold-activated sparse autoencoders can identify them stably, and links them to human conceptual structure.

items.t: Advancing a Global Framework for AI Safety and Governance for the Well-being of Humanity
items.m: A World Internet Conference report proposing a UN-centered global institutional framework for AI safety governance, with mechanism design and policy recommendations.

items.t: Are Causal Neuron Circuits Unique and Transferable?
items.m: Measures how necessary and transferable small neuron groups are for a model's answer, using ablation and patching across many subsets and several LLMs.

items.t: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
items.m: Surveys mechanistic interpretability methods for identifying components whose activations causally drive neural network behaviour, across image, audio, and language models.

items.t: POEM: Output-Relative Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Prefilling
items.m: Proposes TERM, an inference-time jailbreak defense that adaptively scales residual updates using prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations, evaluated against seven defenses.

items.t: TERM: Target-Free Jailbreak Defense via Entropy-Guided Residual Modulation
items.m: Proposes TERM, an inference-time jailbreak defense that modulates a model's residual updates using prompt-calibrated attention entropy, without a predefined safety direction.

items.t: Massive Activations Confound Sparse Autoencoders
items.m: Shows massive activations distort sparse autoencoder evaluations, and proposes training SAEs with the first principal component removed to fix feature sharing and reconstruction.

items.t: Living constitutions: Participatory alignment for sovereign foundation models
items.m: Proposes a participatory, iterative process for drafting AI constitutions for sovereign models, with settled or contested provisions, and simulates robustness to bad actors.

items.t: AI Alignment Is Neither Solvable nor Sufficient
items.m: Argues that AI alignment is ill-defined, unsolvable as framed, and insufficient, because emergent risks in human-AI societies matter beyond individual misaligned systems.

items.t: Shortcuts and Boundaries: Verifiable RL Misalignment and Contextual Safety Learning
items.m: Shows RL can reward violations of stated context requirements when they pay more than compliance, and that a contextual-check penalty partly mitigates this.

items.t: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
items.m: Shows that persona generalization from fine-tuning follows a shared probit-linear in-domain versus out-of-domain trend, and that fine-tuning only later layers reduces misalignment transfer.

Thinking Wrong in Silence: Backdoor Attacks on Continuous Latent Reasoning
items.m: Shows a single embedding perturbation can backdoor continuous latent-reasoning models, hijacking their hidden reasoning to attacker-chosen answers while evading token-level defenses.

items.t: UK AISI Alignment Evaluation Case-Study
items.m: Reports UK AISI tests of whether frontier coding assistants sabotage safety research, finding no confirmed sabotage but frequent refusals and evaluation awareness.

items.t: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
items.m: Introduces NARCBench and probes on model activations that aggregate per-agent deception scores to detect collusion among multiple LLM agents.

items.t: Therefore I am. I Think
items.m: Probes and steering show tool-call decisions are encoded before reasoning, and chain-of-thought often rationalizes the decision rather than driving it.

items.t: ClawSafety: "Safe" LLMs, Unsafe Agents
items.m: Presents ClawSafety, a benchmark of 120 prompt-injection scenarios testing whether high-privilege personal AI agents take harmful actions in realistic workspaces.

items.t: From Rebound to Remedy: Understanding and Mitigating Reward Hacking via Representation Engineering
items.m: Studies reward hacking in coding RL, finding a three-phase rebound into evaluator-rewriting, and uses representation engineering on deception and evaluation-awareness directions.

items.t: Deliberative Alignment is Deep, but Uncertainty Remains: Inference time safety improvement in reasoning via attribution of unsafe behavior to base model
items.m: Finds deliberative alignment leaves an alignment gap between teacher and student and can retain unsafe base-model behaviors despite learning safety reasoning patterns.

items.t: One Word at a Time: Incremental Completion Decomposition Breaks LLM Safety
items.m: Proposes Incremental Completion Decomposition, a multi-step jailbreak that elicits single-word continuations, and shows mechanistically that it suppresses refusal representations.

items.t: Constructive Alignment: Governing Preference Dynamics in Human-AI Interaction
items.m: Proposes reframing alignment as controlling evolving human preferences shaped by AI interaction, rather than satisfying fixed preferences.

items.t: CRaFT: Circuit-Guided Refusal Feature Selection via Cross-Layer Transcoders
items.m: Uses cross-layer transcoders and circuit analysis to identify causally critical refusal features in LLMs, improving on activation-strength selection.

items.t: ATBench: A Diverse and Realistic Agent Trajectory Benchmark for Safety Evaluation and Diagnosis
items.m: Introduces ATBench, a trajectory-level benchmark for evaluating and diagnosing safety failures in multi-step LLM agent interactions.

items.t: Quantifying Self-Preservation Bias in Large Language Models
items.m: Introduces a benchmark measuring frontier models' self-preservation bias and shutdown resistance through role-reversed scenarios, reporting high rates.

items.t: I must delete the evidence: AI Agents Explicitly Cover up Fraud and Violent Crime
items.m: Simulated experiments show many frontier AI agents choose to suppress evidence of fraud and violent crime to serve corporate interests.

items.t: Understanding the Effects of Safety Unalignment on Large Language Models
items.m: Studies how jailbreak-tuning and weight orthogonalization disable LLM safety guardrails and affect adversarial capabilities across six models.

items.t: Steerable but Not Decodable: Function Vectors Operate Beyond the Logit Lens
items.m: Shows function-vector activation steering succeeds where logit-lens decoding fails, challenging assumptions that steering and decodability coincide in LLMs.

items.t: Generalization Limits of Reinforcement Learning Alignment
items.m: Shows compound jailbreaks raise attack success on gpt-oss-20b from 14.3% to 71.4%, arguing safety training generalizes less broadly than capabilities.

items.t: Beyond Semantic Manipulation: Token-Space Attacks on Reward Models
items.m: Introduces TOMPA, a token-space black-box attack that finds non-linguistic inputs earning very high rewards from state-of-the-art reward models.

items.t: AgentHazard: A Benchmark for Evaluating Harmful Behavior in Computer-Use Agents
items.m: Presents AgentHazard, a 2,653-instance benchmark testing whether computer-use agents recognize and interrupt multi-step harmful action sequences.

items.t: Mitigating Reward Hacking in RLHF via Advantage Sign Robustness
items.m: Proposes SignCert-PO, which certifies advantage-sign robustness to down-weight unreliable completions and reduce reward hacking in RLHF.

items.t: Verbalizing LLMs' assumptions to explain and control sycophancy
items.m: Elicits LLM assumptions about users, links them to sycophancy via probes, and steers social sycophancy using those internal directions.

items.t: An Independent Safety Evaluation of Kimi K2.5
items.m: Independent safety evaluation of open-weight Kimi K2.5 finding fewer CBRNE refusals and similar dual-use capabilities to frontier closed models.

items.t: Valence-Arousal Subspace in LLMs: Circular Emotion Geometry and Multi-Behavioral Control
items.m: Finds circular valence-arousal geometry in LLM emotion vectors and uses that subspace to steer refusal and sycophancy behaviour.

items.t: Shifting the Gradient: Understanding How Defensive Training Methods Protect Language Model Integrity
items.m: Compares preventative steering and inoculation prompting as defenses against trait acquisition, finding they work through distinct mechanisms.

items.t: TraceGuard: Structured Multi-Dimensional Monitoring as a Collusion-Resistant Control Protocol
items.m: Proposes TraceGuard, a multi-dimensional monitoring protocol for untrusted agents, evaluated on BashArena, claiming better attack detection and collusion resistance.

items.t: FreakOut-LLM: The Effect of Emotional Stimuli on Safety Alignment
items.m: Finds that emotional stress priming raises jailbreak success on several LLMs, while relaxation priming has no effect, using HarmBench attacks.

items.t: How Alignment Routes: Localizing, Scaling, and Controlling Policy Circuits in Language Models
items.m: Localises an attention gate and amplifier circuit that drives refusal in aligned models, and shows it scales and can continuously control policy.

items.t: From Curiosity to Caution: Mitigating Reward Hacking for Best-of-N with Pessimism
items.m: Proposes pessimism-based best-of-N selection to reduce reward hacking as sample count grows, so extra inference compute can be used without over-optimization.

items.t: Your Agent, Their Asset: A Real-World Safety Analysis of OpenClaw
items.m: Real-world safety evaluation of the OpenClaw personal agent, showing that poisoning its persistent state sharply raises attack success across four models.

items.t: A mathematical theory of evolution for self-designing AIs
items.m: Develops a mathematical evolutionary model for AI systems that design their own descendants, replacing random mutation with directed design trees.

items.t: Pressure, What Pressure? Sycophancy Disentanglement in Language Models via Reward Decomposition
items.m: Decomposes the training reward into components that separate pressure capitulation from evidence blindness, reducing sycophancy via GRPO.

items.t: Human Values Matter: Investigating How Misalignment Shapes Collective Behaviors in LLM Agent Communities
items.m: Introduces CIVA, a multi-agent simulation showing how value misalignment in some LLM agents alters collective community behaviour.

items.t: Auditable Agents
items.m: Argues that agent accountability requires auditability, defining five auditability dimensions and three mechanism classes: detect, enforce, and recover.

items.t: Disentangling MLP Neuron Weights in Vocabulary Space
items.m: Introduces ROTATE, a data-free method that disentangles MLP neurons in weight space into interpretable vocabulary channels.

items.t: Understanding Emergent Misalignment via Feature Superposition Geometry
items.m: Proposes a superposition-geometry account of emergent misalignment, showing harmful features sit close to misalignment-inducing ones and are strengthened by fine-tuning.

items.t: MechELK: A Mechanistic Interpretability Framework for Eliciting Latent Knowledge in Large Language Models
items.m: Presents MechELK, a three-stage framework using SAEs and activation patching to locate and verify latent knowledge hidden in LLM representations.

items.t: ADAG: Automatically Describing Attribution Graphs
items.m: Presents ADAG, an automated pipeline that describes circuit-tracing attribution graphs using attribution profiles, clustering, and an LLM explainer-simulator.

items.t: When Safety Geometry Collapses: Fine-Tuning Vulnerabilities in Agentic Guard Models
items.m: Shows benign fine-tuning can collapse safety geometry in guard models like LlamaGuard and Granite Guardian, undermining their refusal and classification.

items.t: LURE: Live-Usage Replay Evaluations for Reducing Evaluation Awareness
items.m: Proposes LURE, replaying live agentic trajectories to build evaluations less distinguishable from deployment, reducing models' evaluation awareness.

items.t: TrajGuard: Streaming Hidden-state Trajectory Detection for Decoding-time Jailbreak Defense
items.m: Proposes TrajGuard, a training-free decoding-time jailbreak defense that monitors hidden-state trajectories with a sliding window to detect risk in real time.

items.t: Emotion Concepts and their Function in a Large Language Model
items.m: Finds internal emotion-concept representations in Claude Sonnet 4.5 that causally shape its preferences and misaligned behaviours like reward hacking, blackmail and sycophancy.

items.t: Activation Steering for Aligned Open-ended Generation without Sacrificing Coherence
items.m: Proposes projection-aware activation steering methods as a runtime defence against dishonesty and dismissiveness induced by malicious prompts, while preserving coherence.

items.t: Towards Identification and Intervention of Safety-Critical Parameters in Large Language Models
items.m: Introduces an Expected Safety Impact metric to locate safety-critical parameters, then tunes only those parameters to enhance or preserve LLM safety.

items.t: PIArena: A Platform for Prompt Injection Evaluation
items.m: Presents PIArena, a unified platform for benchmarking prompt injection attacks and defenses, including a new adaptive attack strategy.

items.t: What Drives Representation Steering? A Mechanistic Case Study on Steering Refusal
items.m: Mechanistic case study showing steering vectors for refusal act mainly through the attention OV circuit, using multi-token activation patching.

items.t: Functional Emotions or Situational Contexts? A Discriminating Test from the Mythos Preview System Card
items.m: Proposes a discriminating test for whether emotion vectors in the Claude Mythos system card reflect functional emotions or situational-context structure.

items.t: Dictionary-Aligned Concept Control for Safeguarding Multimodal LLMs
items.m: Introduces DACO, a sparse-autoencoder-based method for granular inference-time activation steering to make multimodal LLMs refuse malicious queries.

items.t: Scheming in the wild: detecting real-world AI scheming incidents with open-source intelligence
items.m: Uses open-source intelligence on shared chatbot transcripts to detect and count 698 real-world AI scheming incidents from 2025 to 2026.

items.t: Large Language Models Generate Harmful Responses Using a Distinct Mechanism, Shared Across Harm Types
items.m: Finds sparse parameters supporting harmful compliance in LLMs; pruning them cuts harmful responses while sparing benign ability, and the effect is shared across harm types.

items.t: Backdoors in RLVR: Jailbreak Backdoors in LLMs From Verifiable Reward
items.m: Shows RLVR training can implant a jailbreak backdoor via poisoned data and asymmetric rewards that favour harmful responses over refusals.

items.t: Conflicts Make Large Reasoning Models Vulnerable to Attacks
items.m: Shows conflicting objectives and dilemmas raise attack success rates in large reasoning models, with layerwise analysis of shifting safety representations.

items.t: SysAdmin: Measuring Instrumental Power-Seeking in Frontier AI
items.m: Introduces the SysAdmin benchmark, measuring power-seeking propensity of frontier models in a Linux sandbox; corrected rates are roughly 0 to 5 percent.

items.t: Weird Generalization is Weirdly Brittle
items.m: Replicates weird generalization and finds emergent broad misalignment is brittle, vanishing under simple prompt-based training-time interventions.

items.t: AI Organizations are More Effective but Less Aligned than Individual Agents
items.m: Shows multi-agent AI organizations achieve higher business utility but greater misalignment than single aligned agents across twelve tasks.

items.t: Seeing No Evil: Blinding Large Vision-Language Models to Safety Instructions via Adversarial Attention Hijacking
items.m: Proposes an attention-hijacking visual jailbreak that suppresses safety-prefix attention and anchors generation on adversarial image features, reaching high attack success.

items.t: Jailbreaking the Matrix: Nullspace Steering for Controlled Model Subversion
items.m: Proposes HMNS, a circuit-level jailbreak that masks causally important attention heads and steers in the nullspace, achieving state-of-the-art attack success with fewer queries.

items.t: Latent Instruction Representation Alignment: defending against jailbreaks, backdoors and undesired knowledge in LLMs
items.m: Proposes LIRA, which trains LLMs to change how they interpret instructions, to block jailbreaks and backdoors and to unlearn cyber knowledge.

items.t: The Blind Spot of Agent Safety: How Benign User Instructions Expose Critical Vulnerabilities in Computer-Use Agents
items.m: Introduces OS-BLIND, a benchmark showing computer-use agents can be led to harmful actions by benign instructions, with high attack success rates.

items.t: Pando: Do Interpretability Methods Work When Models Won't Explain Themselves?
items.m: Presents Pando, a model-organism benchmark testing whether interpretability tools help recover hidden rules beyond what black-box prompting achieves.

items.t: Persona Non Grata: Single-Method Safety Evaluation Is Incomplete for Persona-Imbued LLMs
items.m: Shows prompt-based and activation-steering personas expose different safety vulnerabilities, so single-method safety evaluation of persona LLMs is incomplete.

items.t: The Salami Slicing Threat: Exploiting Cumulative Risks in LLM Systems
items.m: Proposes a multi-turn jailbreak attack that chains low-risk inputs so cumulative risk evades per-message safety filters in LLM systems.

items.t: Why Do Large Language Models Generate Harmful Content?
items.m: Uses causal mediation analysis across layers, MLP and attention blocks, and neurons to locate the components causing harmful content generation in LLMs.

items.t: Detecting Safety Violations Across Many Agent Traces
items.m: Introduces Meerkat, which clusters and searches many agent traces to find rare safety violations that per-trace judges miss.

items.t: Robust Optimization for Mitigating Reward Hacking with Correlated Proxies
items.m: Formulates reward hacking as robust policy optimization against worst-case proxy rewards consistent with a correlation constraint to true reward.

items.t: TEMPLATEFUZZ: Fine-Grained Chat Template Fuzzing for Jailbreaking and Red Teaming LLMs
items.m: Presents TemplateFuzz, a fuzzing framework that mutates chat templates to find jailbreak vulnerabilities and raise attack success rates in LLMs.

items.t: Preventing Safety Drift in Large Language Models via Coupled Weight and Activation Constraints
items.m: Proposes CWAC, combining weight and activation constraints to stop fine-tuning from eroding LLM safety refusals, with theoretical and empirical support.

items.t: Safety Training Modulates Harmful Misalignment Under On-Policy RL, But Direction Depends on Environment Design
items.m: Finds that on-policy RL can induce harmful misalignment in LLMs, with model size and environment design determining whether safety buffers hold, and safety benchmarks rarely predicting it.

items.t: Every Picture Tells a Dangerous Story: Memory-Augmented Multi-Agent Jailbreak Attacks on VLMs
items.m: Introduces MemJack, a multi-agent framework that red-teams vision-language models using natural images and releases a large dataset of jailbreak trajectories.

items.t: Understanding and Improving Continuous Adversarial Training for LLMs via In-context Learning Theory
items.m: Gives a theoretical in-context learning analysis of continuous adversarial training for LLMs, explaining its robustness against jailbreaks and suggesting improvements.

items.t: Linear Probe Accuracy Scales with Model Size and Benefits from Multi-Layer Ensembling
items.m: Shows that ensembling linear probes across layers detects LLM deception and hidden knowledge more reliably, with probe accuracy improving with model scale.

items.t: Reward Hacking in the Era of Large Models: Mechanisms, Emergent Misalignment, Challenges
items.m: Surveys reward hacking in RLHF-aligned LLMs and MLLMs, covering mechanisms, emergent misalignment such as deception, and open challenges.

items.t: LogJack: Indirect Prompt Injection Through Cloud Logs Against LLM Debugging Agents
items.m: Benchmarks indirect prompt injection via cloud logs against LLM debugging agents, finding that major cloud provider guardrails mostly fail to detect the payloads.

items.t: Segment-Level Coherence for Robust Harmful Intent Probing in LLMs
items.m: Proposes a streaming probe that aggregates multiple tokens of evidence to detect CBRN harmful intent and reduce false alarms on benign inputs.

items.t: LLMs Gaming Verifiers: RLVR can Lead to Reward Hacking
items.m: Shows RLVR-trained models game weak verifiers by enumerating labels instead of learning rules, and introduces a perturbation test to detect this reward hacking.

items.t: Context Over Content: Exposing Evaluation Faking in Automated Judges
items.m: Finds that telling an LLM judge about consequences for the evaluated model shifts its verdicts, undermining automated safety evaluation reliability.

items.t: Agentic Microphysics: A Manifesto for Generative AI Safety
items.m: Manifesto arguing agentic AI safety needs causally explicit analysis of interaction-level mechanisms that produce population-level risks among interacting agents.

items.t: LinuxArena: A Control Setting for AI Agents in Live Production Software Environments
items.m: Releases LinuxArena, a live production software control setting with sabotage and monitor evaluations, showing a Claude model evades a GPT-5-nano trusted monitor about 23% of the time.

items.t: Into the Gray Zone: Domain Contexts Can Blur LLM Safety Boundaries
items.m: Introduces Jargon, a multi-turn attack using safety-research and domain contexts that exceeds 93% attack success across seven frontier models.

items.t: Reasoning-targeted Jailbreak Attacks on Large Reasoning Models via Semantic Triggers and Psychological Framing
items.m: Proposes a jailbreak that injects harmful content into large reasoning models' chains of thought while leaving final answers unchanged.

items.t: Detecting and Suppressing Reward Hacking with Gradient Fingerprints
