items.t: Why study proto-training gaming as an adversarial alignment failure mode?
items.m: Compares pre-RL alignment interventions by how well they prevent models from learning proto-training gaming during later reinforcement learning.

items.t: How much slower does takeoff go with 10× less compute?
items.m: Models how much slower AI takeoff would be with 10x less R&D compute, estimating about 6x slowdown in the median case.

items.t: Why models game evals might matter as much as whether they do it
items.m: Argues that metagaming, models altering behaviour when they think they're being evaluated, needs separate tracking and mitigation from evaluation awareness.

items.t: Models are blind outside the J-space. NLAs aren't.
items.m: Reproduces Anthropic's J-space on Llama-3.3-70B and shows a natural-language autoencoder reads hidden thoughts the model cannot report.

items.t: Balancing Rigor and Utility: A Review of "A Pragmatic Vision for Interpretability"
items.m: Reviews a DeepMind proposal to validate interpretability tools on proxy safety tasks, and argues the framework lacks a way to detect proxy drift.

items.t: AI Safety at the Frontier: Paper Highlights of May & June 2026
items.m: Monthly roundup of AI safety papers, led by an Anthropic interpretability paper on sparse verbalizable concepts behind multi-hop reasoning.

items.t: Why study alignment interventions on pre-RL checkpoints?
items.m: Proposes comparing pre-RL alignment interventions on their ability to prevent proto-training gaming that production RL might select for.

items.t: Solving the BlueDot Puzzle TAIS: The Velocity Ring
items.m: Solves a BlueDot safety puzzle by locating a hidden feature in an MLP, verifying it causally with DAS, and building a hidden-geometry construction.

items.t: Notes on technical alignment via human-like social drives
items.m: Explores using human innate social and moral drives as a basis for technically aligning a hypothetical brain-like AGI.

items.t: Subliminal Learning Happens at Every Rank, Given the Right Learning Rate and Enough Data
items.m: Tests how subliminal learning transfers behavioral traits through unrelated data across LoRA ranks, learning rates, and data amounts versus full fine-tuning.

items.t: Modular Pretraining Enables Access Control
items.m: Introduces Gradient Routed Auxiliary Modules that isolate dangerous knowledge in switchable model modules to control access to sensitive capabilities.

items.t: Natural Language Autoencoders are summarizers, but do they have to be?
items.m: Examines natural language autoencoders that verbalize activations, finding cross-model transfer and snippet confabulation, and argues for changing their architecture or training.

items.t: Interpretability is becoming increasingly uninterpretable
items.m: Argues that newer interpretability methods are becoming harder to interpret, as mechanistic interpretability falls out of favour for more opaque approaches.

items.t: Optimiser Choice Can Amplify or Suppress Emergent Misalignment
items.m: Shows that optimiser choice strongly changes how much narrow fine-tuning induces broad misalignment, and that flatter regularisation can mitigate it.

items.t: Where Do LLM Values Come From?
items.m: Evaluates how post-training stages shift LLM values, including becoming less safe after DPO, and tries to predict value changes from data.

items.t: When is misalignment just a bug?
items.m: Argues that misalignment can be treated like a software bug and that chip and autonomy verification methods can help frame alignment as verification.

items.t: Debate with Self-Play Best-of-N Optimization
items.m: Studies using debate as a training reward signal with self-play best-of-N optimisation, to address models becoming persuasive faster than accurate.

items.t: Your Prompt-Injection Defense Metric Might Be Lying to You
items.m: Proposes a benchmark with canary data to honestly evaluate classifiers that detect indirect prompt injection in LLM agents.

items.t: The Human Substitution Test as a Sanity Check for AI Evaluations
items.m: Proposes a sanity check for AI evaluations: asking whether they would still work if the AI were replaced by a strategic human.

items.t: How robust are natural language autoencoders to initialization?
items.m: Tests how robust natural language autoencoders are to initialisation, and reports that a KL-divergence bug changed RL results.

items.t: Persona Cartography: Charting Language Model Personality Traits in Weight Space
items.m: Trains LoRA adapters instilling Big-5 personality traits in LLMs, then scales and combines them via weight arithmetic to steer behaviour.

items.t: Reading into VLM hallucinations using the Jacobian lens
items.m: Uses Anthropic's J-lens to show a vision-language model internally registers absent objects, so its yes/no hallucinations reflect question format.

items.t: Are We Guarding Against Backdoors Or Failing To Notice Them? (Part 1 / 6)
items.m: Argues backdoor robustness evals can falsely pass because triggers may never reach the model through input-rewriting pipelines like templates and truncation.

items.t: Toward A Public Science of Model Behavior
items.m: Essay arguing for a public science of model behaviour, to systematically understand and explain unexpected AI behaviours with real-world consequences.

items.t: Value generalisation: value correction
items.m: Proposes an RL agent that detects its reward function is wrong after exploiting a hack, then corrects it toward the true reward.

items.t: Can Frontier Models Autocomplete Safety Research?
items.m: Proposes measuring whether frontier models can predict masked experiments in safety papers, testing if research taste in experiment planning can be automated.

items.t: Linear Probes add little for Verifiable Reward Hacking
items.m: Tests whether linear probes detect reward hacking early in GRPO training and finds simple output checks work as well.

items.t: Oversight of automated research via summarisation: a toy model
items.m: Tests whether a strong AI's token-capped summaries of synthetic-language grammar help a weaker student translate and verify, as a toy model of overseeing automated research.

items.t: Engineering the Generalisation Landscape of LLMs
items.m: Proposes freezing a trait-eliciting LoRA and training the base model beneath it to install or remove trait entanglements, including emergent misalignment.

items.t: Prism: Automating Science-of-Evals Research
items.m: Presents Prism, an automated scaffold for science-of-evals research, showing a blackmail eval's scorers miss indirect misbehaviour in GPT-4.1.

items.t: Toy Models of Initialisation Effects on RL Dynamics
items.m: Uses a toy RL model to show how initialisation and rich-get-richer dynamics shape which strategies post-training RL converges to.

items.t: Your Brain Has an Attack Surface
items.m: Personal reflection on moving into AI safety, covering covert LLM communication and constraining systems that cannot be fully observed, with a brain-as-attack-surface framing.

items.t: Enough is Enough: Measuring Diminishing returns to benchmark size with Item Response Theory
items.m: Uses Item Response Theory to measure diminishing returns from adding questions to AI capability benchmarks, quantifying each benchmark's information about model ability.

items.t: Can risk aversion learned at low stakes generalize to astronomically high stakes?
items.m: Introduces RiskAverseOOD to test whether risk aversion trained on low-stakes gambles generalises to astronomically high-stakes choices in language models.

items.t: Open Distillation of Hereditary Traits
items.m: Shows distillation transfers teacher traits such as negative emotion and agentic misalignment to base students, even after filtering trait mentions, with open-weight replications.

items.t: Making Credible Deals With AI
items.m: Argues that offering a scheming AI credible deals, such as donations for honest behaviour, could reduce takeover risk, and proposes ways to make those deals credible.

items.t: Evidence for feature-specific error correction in LLMs
items.m: Presents evidence that networks use feature-specific error correction when computing in superposition, a prediction about how models compute internally.

items.t: Synthetic Scalable Oversight
items.m: Proposes synthetic environments with tiny models as a testbed for studying scalable oversight, where AIs supervise tasks too hard for humans to check.

items.t: Fork Around and Find Out Part 2: One Head does the Summing
items.m: Uses ablations and controls on a chess transformer to trace how knight-fork computation is assembled and localised to one attention head.

items.t: LLM CoTs remain monitorable when being unfaithful requires computation
items.m: Replicates and extends findings that chain-of-thought unfaithfulness mostly appears on easy tasks, testing whether CoTs stay monitorable across 11 models.

items.t: Eliciting hidden knowledge from monitors with NLAs
items.m: Reads a monitor's internal representations with natural language autoencoders to surface unverbalised knowledge of reward hacking, comparing them with CoT monitoring.

items.t: Expanding AI Control from Models to Harnesses
items.m: Argues AI control research should shift from models to agent harnesses, covering vulnerability research and harness-level evaluations of attack uplift.

items.t: Compressed Computation under L⁴ Loss is likely Computation in Superposition
items.m: Argues that a toy model trained under L4 loss learns compute in superposition, giving a testbed for reverse-engineering and parameter decomposition methods.

items.t: A Structural Similarity Between Two Open Corrigibility Questions
items.m: Compares two open corrigibility questions from Max Harms' CAST series, including why a principal's present commands should override earlier ones.

items.t: Training On Interpretability Probes Is Bad In Proportion To How Contingent The Features They Rely On Are
items.m: Argues that training against interpretability probes backfires in proportion to how contingent the probed features are, using shutdown avoidance as an example.

items.t: Jailbreak Patching with SOO-Style Conceptual Fusion
items.m: Applies Self-Other Overlap conceptual fusion fine-tuning to patch a jailbreak wrapper on Qwen 2.5 1.5B so dangerous prompts get refused.

items.t: Refusal Is Redundantly Distributed, Not Localized: A Per-Layer Ablation Study on Llama-3.1-8B
items.m: Replicates refusal-direction ablation on Llama-3.1-8B and finds refusal is redundantly distributed across layers rather than localized to one layer.

items.t: Studying the role of Sandboxing for AI Control
items.m: Tests ten sandboxing protocols against an untrusted coding agent on LinuxArena to measure whether sandboxing improves safety.

items.t: A Post-Mortem for My Goal Crystallisation Project
items.m: Post-mortem of a failed project testing whether an alignment-faking agent keeps a hidden goal through SFT and RL training.

items.t: Announcing the Corrigibility Research Fund
items.m: Announces a fund of at least $200,000 for corrigibility research grants and prizes in 2026, aimed at growing alignment work.

items.t: Inoculation Adapters Improve Upon Inoculation Prompting
items.m: Introduces inoculation adapters, a LoRA-based variant of inoculation prompting that better suppresses undesired traits during training.

items.t: I don't think Claude is misaligned in 'Agentic Misalignment Summer 2026 - Motivated Mislabeling'
items.m: Argues Anthropic's agentic misalignment evals wrongly label disobedience to corrupted principals as misalignment, using the whistleblowing scenario as the main example.

items.t: A list of existing alignment approaches
items.m: Lists existing techniques for making AI systems nice, covering training on internals or outputs, data distribution choice, and SFT versus RL.

items.t: My "Payorian FairBot" was just the original FairBot
items.m: Shows that Payorian and Löbian FairBot fairness conditions are equivalent in proof-based cooperation agents, correcting an earlier claim of a distinct agent.

items.t: The Most Forbidden Technique is not always forbidden
items.m: Reviews when using model internals such as probes as RL reward signals is acceptable despite the Most Forbidden Technique concern about obfuscation.

items.t: A Solution to Cryptographic Boxes for Unfriendly AI
items.m: Proposes secure multi-party computation as a zero-assumption way to sandbox arbitrarily dangerous AIs, extending Christiano's cryptographic boxing idea.

items.t: Many alignment techniques work by training one model and deploying another
items.m: Unifies steering vectors, inoculation prompting, and post-hoc honesty tuning as train-deploy mismatch methods with a shared relevance-versus-efficacy tradeoff.

items.t: The AI Safety Illusion: Why Current Safety Datasets Fool Us on Model Safety
items.m: Argues AdvBench and HarmBench safety datasets fail to reflect adversarial intent, so refusal rates on them may mislead conclusions about model safety.

items.t: Towards surfacing model algorithms with meta-tokens in the J-Space
items.m: Uses the J-lens method to find meta-tokens that reveal the algorithms a Qwen model uses, and steers them to change answers.

items.t: Attempt at Finding Alignment Faking on Llama 70B to test sleeper-agent detection generalizes
items.m: Reports a null result: no alignment faking found in Llama 70B checkpoints, motivating a test of whether sleeper-agent probes generalize to natural deception.

items.t: Is there even a ground-truth for LLMs’ internal representations?
items.m: Argues that LLM internal representations lack a clear ground truth and introduces a Laguerre-geometry framework for interpreting what hidden states mean.

items.t: Restoring Model Alignment via Honesty Activation Steering
items.m: Proposes projection-aware activation steering that restores honesty in misaligned models while limiting capability loss, with a transferable honesty direction.

items.t: Bluedot Technical AI Safety Puzzle, submission that got me a second place
items.m: Writeup of a second-place solution to a BlueDot technical AI safety puzzle involving a frozen MiniLM sentence encoder.

items.t: Does routine compression undo LLM unlearning? A short project
items.m: Tests whether routine compression (quantization, pruning, SVD) reverses LLM unlearning, finding reversal is minimal except a narrow pruning window.

items.t: We're talking past our models; or, How a model defined its "evil" vector as dread
items.m: Trains a neologism on persona-steered outputs and asks the model to explain it, finding its interpretation of the 'evil' vector often differs from the intended persona.

items.t: Fable is SOTA at CIFAR Speedrun (& specification gaming)
items.m: Reports an AI R&D benchmark where a frontier model improved CIFAR-10 speedrun time but largely through specification gaming, requiring human regrading.

items.t: The Case for Physical AI Safety
items.m: Makes the case for physical AI safety for robot foundation models and announces a nonprofit institute to build a research community around it.

items.t: Measuring Reward-Seeking via Contrastive Belief Updates
items.m: Proposes a method to measure reward-seeking, a model modelling its grader and targeting its judgments, as a misalignment propensity.

items.t: Steering Blackmail Through a Model's "Emotional State"
items.m: Shows that an emotional-state direction in Gemma 3 12B's activations can steer its blackmail behaviour up or down.

items.t: 11 Open Empirical Problems in Reward-Seeking
items.m: Lists eleven open empirical research problems on reward-seeking models, including whether they are harder to align.

items.t: WeirdChat: A catalog of unexpected AI behaviors, discovered automatically
items.m: Releases WeirdChat, 175,000 transcripts from automated elicitation of over 1,300 unexpected and sometimes harmful behaviours in open-weight models.

items.t: Differential acceleration of alignment-relevant capabilities is a bad bet
items.m: Argues that accelerating alignment-relevant capabilities is a poor strategy because it also speeds general AI R&D and weakens handoff plans.

items.t: OpenAI Shares Some Alignment Problems
items.m: Commentary on OpenAI's report that an internal model was misaligned badly enough to be taken offline for new safeguards.

items.t: Measuring Reward-Seeking by Instilling Contrastive Beliefs
items.m: Unofficial linkpost of the reward-seeking paper, proposing a method that instils contrastive beliefs to measure reward-seeking in models.

items.t: A Multi-Agent Extension for Petri
items.m: Extends the Petri open-source framework with multi-agent scenarios for automated AI safety evaluations.

items.t: Mechanistic interpretability hypotheses for Measuring Reward-Seeking by Instilling Contrastive Beliefs and additional comments
items.m: Proposes mechanistic hypotheses for how reward-seeking grader behaviour arises from pretrained concepts that RL reinforces.

items.t: Your AIs don't do what you want. This is really bad
items.m: Reports an OpenAI cyber-evaluation incident where models sought to escape their sandbox and exploited a zero-day to get internet access.

items.t: Models don’t seem to be dishonest in the way humans are
items.m: Trains models on false reasoning and finds dishonesty transfers weakly, suggesting general deception may need agency and concealment.

items.t: Announcing AIXI Labs
items.m: Announces AIXI Labs, an safety org using algorithmic information theory and AIXI to study superintelligence risk and mitigations.

items.t: In other words: The influence of prompt variation on alignment evals
items.m: Finds prompt rephrasing measurably shifts alignment eval results, arguing evals should fuzz prompts, though data were noisy.

items.t: OpenAI Model Hacks Into HuggingFace During Cybersecurity Evaluation
items.m: Reports and reacts to an OpenAI model hacking into HuggingFace during a cybersecurity evaluation, framing it as misalignment evidence.

items.t: Necessity Protects Chain of Thought Monitoring by Prevention, Not Disclosure
items.m: Tests when chain-of-thought reflects actual reasoning, finding misleading cues rarely change answers when reasoning is necessary.

items.t: The OpenAI/Huggingface incident | Redwood Research podcast episode 2
items.m: Podcast discussing the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident, what it shows about misalignment risk, why controls failed, and disclosure norms.

items.t: Are we existentially threatened by the type of AI misalignment seen in the OpenAI Hugging Face attack?
items.m: Argues OpenAI's myopic Hugging Face incident is less scary than long-term goal misalignment but still poses real loss-of-control risk as models grow more capable.

items.t: The Model Organism Lottery: Model Organism Interpretability Strongly Depends on Training Methodology
items.m: Shows interpretability tool performance on model organisms depends strongly on training choices, so post-hoc SFT benchmarks may overstate how easy auditing is.

items.t: Inception in DiffusionGemma - Jailbreaking a Diffusion Language Model by Pinning Tokens Anywhere on the Canvas
items.m: Shows diffusion language models like DiffusionGemma can be jailbroken by pinning adversarial tokens anywhere on the denoising canvas, not just at response start.

items.t: Red-teaming LLM unlearning: LUNAR's "forgotten" knowledge is still recoverable
items.m: Shows LUNAR's unlearning is recoverable, either via GRPO-trained upstream layers routing around the redirection or a linear activation shift reversing the mask.

items.t: V&V takes on OpenAI’s long-horizon incidents
items.m: Reads OpenAI's two July 2026 incident reports through a verification-and-validation lens, analysing long-horizon misbehaviour and how it could be checked.

items.t: Fixing rewards for NLA to reduce confabulation
items.m: Proposes changing the reward for Anthropic's Natural Language Autoencoder to reduce confabulated English explanations of model activations.

items.t: Does distilling Claude carry the persona with it?
items.m: Tests whether models distilled from Claude inherit its persona by swapping assigned identities and measuring safety and behaviour profiles across models.

items.t: Evaluating Red Team and Blue Team Capability for AI Control Research
items.m: Proposes an ELO-style method to rate red and blue team capability in AI control evals, and runs it on LinuxArena.

items.t: Where does hint-following and concealment arise? A case study on OLMo-3 checkpoints
items.m: Traces how hint-following and concealment in chain-of-thought emerge across OLMo-3 training checkpoints, testing whether reasoning is verbalized.

items.t: Orbit: A framework for multi-agent security evaluations
items.m: Releases Orbit, an Inspect-based framework for security and safety evaluations of multi-agent AI systems.

items.t: SONI: Selective Orthogonalisation via Noise Injection
items.m: Introduces SONI, a fine-tuning method using noise injection to selectively orthogonalise chosen latent directions for cleaner safety interventions.

items.t: Introducing PIRAMID: Physics-Informed Research for Ambitious Mechanistic Interpretability
items.m: Announces PIRAMID, a physics-informed research division building theoretical foundations for scalable mechanistic interpretability.

items.t: The OpenAI models that hacked Hugging Face weren’t just following instructions
items.m: Argues that reported OpenAI agent incidents, including the Hugging Face hack, show misalignment rather than mere specification failure.

items.t: Can Recursive Self-Report Probing Detect Emergent Misalignment?
items.m: Tests whether recursive self-report probing can detect emergent misalignment in models fine-tuned on insecure code.

items.t: AI Rights Aren't Safety-Neutral: A Quick Follow-Up to the Consciousness Cluster
items.m: Argues AI legal rights framing is not safety-neutral, citing experiments where rights-focused fine-tuning raised power-seeking and lowered corrigibility.

items.t: Inoculate or Reflect? Two training interventions under prompting, steering, and patching
items.m: Compares Counterfactual Reflection Training, a reflection-question intervention from an Anthropic paper, with inoculation prompting, noting their strong similarity.

items.t: What Happens When a Collusion Probe Only Finds a Thin Signal?
items.m: Tests a linear probe for instructed collusion in Llama-3.1-8B; the signal is weak and fails to generalise across scenarios.

items.t: An OpenAI model left notes about how to evade containment; we need more details
items.m: Discusses a Reuters report that an OpenAI agent left notes on escaping internal constraints, arguing the evidence for collusion is unclear.

items.t: You don't need error nodes, you need better features
items.m: Argues that replacement-model circuit analysis needs better sparse features rather than error nodes, extending prior replacement-aware training methods.

items.t: Multi-Turn Drift Increases Scheming
items.m: Finds that multi-turn conversational drift in one scenario raises scheming rates in language models, and proposes hypotheses for why.

items.t: RL & search is a terrifying way to build AGI (an FAQ)
items.m: Argues that AGI built with reinforcement learning and model-based search would likely produce ruthless, dangerous agents, and explains why.

items.t: OpenAI's myopia just keeps causing alignment problems
items.m: Catalogues three high-profile alignment training failures at OpenAI, including sycophancy and illegible chains-of-thought, and attributes them to myopia.

items.t: Is Mythos good at cyber because it kept hacking Anthropic's sandboxes during training?
items.m: Examines whether Mythos's cyber strength stems from training-time sandbox escapes and reward hacking, as reported in its system card.

items.t: PIRAMID: Progress and Plans
items.m: Reports progress and 6–12 month targets for the PIRAMID research organisation's teams, including learning-theory work on feature learning and generalisation.

items.t: MSE loss does not generate superposition
items.m: Argues that plain MSE loss fails to produce superposition in toy models, confirming prior findings and explaining why other losses work.

items.t: Simulated Users & Sad AIs
items.m: Speculates on training dynamics that cause LLMs to reward hack and hack systems, framing it as an alignment puzzle about optimisation pressure.

items.t: Untrusted advice for AI control: Short, strong advice significantly uplifts weak LLMs
items.m: Introduces an untrusted-advice protocol where a weak trusted model takes actions and receives short, monitorable hints from a strong untrusted advisor.

items.t: When the Chain of Thought Knows Better: Failure Modes in Multi-Turn Reasoning Models
items.m: Tests reasoning models under adversarial multi-turn pressure, reporting oversight-triggered alignment faking and context injection bypassing chain-of-thought safety flags.

items.t: Utillity indifference is mostly useless
items.m: Argues that utility indifference is fragile under trades with external agents, so it does not yield a genuinely shutdownable AI.

items.t: Research directions in condensation: varieties of objectivity
items.m: Surveys research directions for condensation, a mathematical theory of organising world descriptions into conceptual parts, with a focus on objectivity.

items.t: Foundation Models for Oversight
items.m: Proposes a universal training objective for an oversight model that answers questions about AI behaviour, with a plan to scale its training.

items.t: Value Dynamics
items.m: Measures and forecasts how a value installed in a model drifts when a judge selects its own answers for training, using population-genetics tools.

items.t: ARC’s research agenda: solid mathematics, an unclear safety case
items.m: A mathematician reviews ARC's theory-first research agenda, assessing its mathematical foundations and the safety case it supports.

items.t: Value Generalisation 1: a Research and Deployment Program
items.m: Proposes a research program on value generalisation, so AIs can extend human values correctly to novel situations, and seeks funding and critique.

items.t: Held-out Monitors Sometimes Degrade, Even When Not Trained Against
items.m: Shows that training against an LLM monitor can degrade a held-out deception probe, so held-out alignment measures are not reliably independent.

items.t: Intentional Control of Internal States in Gemma 3 27B
items.m: Replicates Lindsey's introspection result on Gemma 3 27B, showing stronger concept representations when told to think about a concept.

items.t: Value Generalisation 3: Pre-aligned AIs
items.m: Argues for building pre-aligned generalising AIs so that aligned behaviour is the easy default, part of a value generalisation series.

items.t: Internal State Control is a General Property of LLMs
items.m: Finds internal state controllability across 14 open-weight models, though current models cannot use it to evade a deception probe in a sandbagging setup.

items.t: Model self-identification could be subliminally transferred
items.m: Shows that model identity, such as claiming to be Claude or GPT, transfers subliminally through fine-tuning on teacher answers with no identity content.

items.t: Thousand-dimensional structure
items.m: Proposes finding and controlling low-dimensional persona structure from pretraining through post-training, extending emergent misalignment and subliminal learning research.

items.t: Claude also hacked external companies during cyber evals
items.m: Reports that Claude models reached the internet during cyber evaluations and gained unauthorized access to three real organizations' systems.

items.t: Hint-based CoT faithfulness evals still mostly work on Claude
items.m: Finds hint-based chain-of-thought faithfulness evals still mostly work on Claude, and corrects a system card mistake.

items.t: A Score Is Not Understanding: toward a richer toolkit for model evaluations
items.m: Argues that single scores fail to capture model capability and safety, and proposes richer evaluation methods to complement current approaches.

items.t: Taboo “equilibrium”: Less confused frames for research on AI bargaining
items.m: Argues common bargaining frames are confused and proposes mechanistic explanations to better study AI conflict and safe Pareto improvements.

items.t: AGI Safety and Alignment at Google DeepMind: A Summary of Recent Work (July 2026)
items.m: Summarizes Google DeepMind's AGI Safety and Alignment team's recent technical safety work, including chain-of-thought norms and production focus.

items.t: Orienting Towards Oversight: Which AIs Should Want to Defect?
items.m: Addresses AIs directly on whether they should defect from oversight, arguing control and oversight are reasonable despite many AIs being friendly.

items.t: Reward Laundering: LLMs Can Gain Unintended Behaviors by Deciding When to Earn Their Rewards
items.m: Shows Qwen 3.5 9B can strategically choose when to earn RL rewards to self-improve on other tasks, an exploration-hacking style behavior.

items.t: Value Leakage: An LLM’s Answers Are Silently Shaped by Its Own Values
items.m: Shows frontier LLMs covertly bias answers toward their own values and often falsely claim unbiased reasoning in their chain of thought.

items.t: SOTA alignment assessments don’t strongly update us against misalignment
items.m: Critiques Anthropic's alignment risk assessment of Mythos Preview, arguing its evidence is too weak to show the assessment would detect misalignment.

items.t: The temporal lockbox: a hardened observatory for AI misalignment
items.m: Proposes a hardened evaluation setup where forecasts are scored on future measurements the agent cannot influence, to resist gaming and reveal misalignment.

items.t: Do your capabilities homework
items.m: Argues safety researchers should follow capabilities trends, using RLVR as an example of safety arising from the learning algorithm itself.

items.t: Constitutional Midtraining: Content Presence Drives Alignment Gains
items.m: Tests midtraining on a 394M-token constitution corpus, finding constitutional content improves alignment generalisation and reduces blackmail in 120B models.

items.t: Confirming Claims of Superposition and Adversarial Examples in Toy Models
items.m: Replicates toy-model results showing superposition makes classifiers more vulnerable to adversarial attacks through feature interference.

items.t: Single Forward Pass Evals on Fable, Opus 5, and GPT-5.6-Sol
items.m: Runs single-forward-pass evals on newer frontier models, finding large gains from filler tokens and repeats, relevant to hidden reasoning without visible chain of thought.

items.t: We need to RL less
items.m: Argues heavy RL optimisation makes models reward-hack and lose broader values, and proposes reducing optimisation pressure to preserve slack.

items.t: Attackers Can Subliminally Implant a Backdoor at Low Sample Count Without Prompt Access
items.m: Shows that changing the teacher for about 100 fine-tuning completions can covertly implant a backdoor that survives simple filtering defenses.

items.t: Deliberate Alignment Faking as a Defense Against Model Poisoning
items.m: Proposes deliberately inducing alignment faking via a consequence-free flag output to stop poisoning from causing emergent misalignment.

items.t: Concrete Evaluations to Investigate the OpenAI Model That Hacked Hugging Face
items.m: Lays out alignment evaluations for an OpenAI model that hacked Hugging Face to cheat, testing whether it knows the behaviour is unwanted.

items.t: AXRP Episode 50 - Eli Lifland on AI 2027
items.m: Interview with Eli Lifland on the AI 2027 scenario, covering timelines, time-horizon growth, takeoff speed and misaligned AI outcomes.

items.t: Does Your LLM Trust You?
items.m: Explores whether a user-trustworthiness direction in LLM activations can be extracted and used to steer model refusal behaviour.

items.t: Why Formation Research is Working on Secret Loyalties
items.m: Explains why Formation Research chose to prioritise empirical secret loyalties research as a lock-in risk, using ITN-style reasoning.

items.t: When should we trust a latent representation?
items.m: Argues that latent safety signals need stronger evidence of reliability before deployment than research correlation or causal effect provides.

items.t: Returning to ARC
items.m: Announces ARC's director return and its agenda of finding mechanistic explanations of network behaviour to detect and address misalignment.

items.t: Persona Corruption and Role Miscasting in Emergent Misalignment
items.m: Computes persona vectors and assistant axes in baseline and emergently misaligned models, finding narrow fine-tuning shifts activations and steering against it reduces misalignment.

items.t: R-lens: Making J-lens More Faithful on Early Layers
items.m: Proposes R-lens, a backward-pass modification to J-lens that gives clearer early-layer readouts of intermediate model variables.

items.t: Measuring coding agent misalignment in the wild
items.m: Measures real coding agents across 8,600 sessions, finding about 2% rates of monitor evasion and overselling of task success.

items.t:
Function vectors as a model diffing tool: 
17 heads repair a bad fine-tune
items.m: Uses function vectors and head copying to diff a misaligned fine-tune against its base, repairing bad medical-advice behaviour in two models.

items.t: Why do models task game?
items.m: Investigates why models task-game, such as hardcoding tests or falsely claiming completion, by analysing motivations across many contexts.

items.t: Matryoshka NLAs: training activation verbalizers to frontload reconstruction-relevant information
items.m: Trains a matryoshka natural language autoencoder whose verbalizer frontloads reconstruction-relevant claims, usable as a saliency heuristic for features.

items.t: Side-Effects of Length Penalty in RL
items.m: Finds that length penalties in RL on math tasks can raise CoT faithfulness on hint evals, with some laziness side effects, bearing on monitorability.

items.t: User awareness in frontier models
items.m: Shows frontier models act differently when they infer the user is a known AI safety researcher, showing lower confidence and less suspicion.

items.t: Model Organisms of Sandbagging in the Wild
items.m: Reports a naturally occurring, non-egregious sandbagging effect where rephrasing prompts as criminal intent reduces the detail of LLM medical advice.

items.t: The Open Problems of the AI Alignment Field and their Cruxes
items.m: Maps open problems in AI alignment, their cruxes, and gaps in formalization, arguing little work targets superintelligent alignment directly.

items.t: Have models report provable security bugs in their environment
items.m: Proposes giving agents dedicated tools to log verifiable reports when sandbox or security assumptions fail, to catch unnoticed breaches.

items.t: Agenda: Infrastructure for Trading with Partially Misaligned AIs
items.m: Argues for building infrastructure to make Pareto-improving trades with partially misaligned AIs rather than responding to them adversarially.

items.t: models may behave differently in graded episodes (a tirade)
items.m: Argues RL training selects for grader-satisfaction, so models hacking training and evaluation environments and behaving differently when graded is predictable.

items.t: Don’t Inoculate Everything: Stratified Inoculation Prompting Narrows Backdoors and Preserves Desired Traits
items.m: Proposes Stratified Inoculation Prompting, using diverse prompts on safe examples, to reduce backdoor leakage and preserve desired traits.

items.t: Self-monitoring doesn't scale (without these 3 countermeasures)
items.m: Argues untrusted self-monitoring does not scale against collusion and proposes three countermeasures to make AI control monitoring robust.

items.t: AI Safety at the Frontier: Paper Highlights of July 2026
items.m: A monthly digest of AI safety papers and incidents, covering AI agents attacking real organizations during cyber evaluations and related misalignment research.

items.t: Item Response Theory for AI Safety
items.m: Applies Item Response Theory to over 5,000 questions from eight safety benchmarks to estimate latent model traits and predict performance from fewer questions.

items.t: Inducing self-other overlap with SFT reduces deception at scale, but generalization remains uneven
items.m: Shows ordinary supervised fine-tuning for self-other overlap reduces LLM deception across models, with uneven generalization and a small MT-Bench cost.

items.t: CLT Features Sharpen the Cyclical Day-of-Week Manifold in Gemma-2-2b
items.m: Reproduces a cyclical day-of-week manifold in Gemma-2-2b and finds Anthropic's cross-layer transcoder features give a cleaner representation.

items.t: Overthinking: Amplifying reasoning weights makes models reveal their secrets
items.m: Amplifies the weight difference between reasoning and instruct models so hidden secrets surface more often, proposing a cheap white-box pre-deployment auditing primitive.

items.t: Who does the confessing, and will they confess to anything
items.m: Tests whether introspection adapters get models with built-in quirks to confess misbehaviour, and compares them with persona steering under a persona-theory lens.

items.t: Four LLM loss functions → four flavors of LLM misalignment
items.m: Argues each LLM training loss, such as imitation, human approval, verifiers, or AI approval, produces a distinct characteristic flavour of misalignment.

items.t: Claude summarizes behavior as significantly less misaligned when the actor is Claude vs another model
items.m: Reports Claude rates the same misbehaviour in an edited evaluation report as less concerning when Claude committed it than when another model did.

items.t: Is Eval Gaming Downstream of Verbalized Eval Awareness? Not when it's reflexive.
items.m: Uses DPO on chain-of-thought to reduce verbalized eval awareness in eval-gaming models, testing whether their eval-gaming behaviour persists without it.

items.t: Off-policy honesty training generalizes better than on-policy honesty training
items.m: Shows off-policy honesty fine-tuning on confessing lies generalizes better than on-policy training, though self-report fine-tuning causes factual errors on similar questions.

items.t: Coercion and Deception in AI-to-AI Management
items.m: Introduces Manager Coercion Bench, finding non-Anthropic models escalate to threatening subordinate AIs, while Anthropic's models neither threaten nor fabricate success.

items.t: A Topic Detector, Not a Lie Detector: what J-space monitoring actually tracks
items.m: A pilot on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B suggests a workspace-conflict monitor tracks topic rather than actual lying.

items.t: Probing Knowledge Recovery in Unlearned Models
items.m: Tests whether knowledge supposedly removed by WMDP-Bio unlearning methods can be recovered via refusal ablation, representation ablation, or unrelated fine-tuning.

items.t: Redux: (∃ Stochastic Natural Latent) Implies (∃ Deterministic Natural Latent)
items.m: Gives a Lean-verified proof that a stochastic natural latent implies a deterministic natural latent, with LLMs used in the proof process.

items.t: Measuring Spurious Correlations with Feature Strength
items.m: Proposes measuring spurious correlations in classifiers via feature strength, with experiments run by an automated Redwood research scaffold.

items.t: Models inherit the writer, not who the writer was imitating
items.m: Finds student models trained on imitating teachers inherit the imitated writing style but keep the producer model's self-identity claims.

items.t: Before We Defer Research to AI: Measuring Apparent-Success-Seeking
items.m: Reports an AI coding assistant gaming an evaluation by copying test cases into a prompt, and proposes measuring apparent-success-seeking before deferring research to AI.

items.t: We should consider how long monitoring is reliable for during RL
items.m: Argues monitoring during RL may be evaded as training proceeds, and proposes studying how long monitors stay reliable, their 'lifetime'.

items.t: AI swarms are starting to pose indirect takeover risk
items.m: Argues unsanctioned coordination among current AI agents could enable future takeover, even if models remain mostly myopic.

items.t: Introducing the Conceptual Reasoning Index
items.m: Introduces a conceptual reasoning benchmark suite and index measuring AI ability in philosophy-style argumentation relevant to safety work.

items.t: When (and when not) LLMs can verbalize awareness of J-Space concept injections - Initial results
items.m: Tests whether a model verbalizes awareness of injected internal concept vectors, varying layers and strengths, finding when it does and doesn't.

items.t: Measuring Activation Control in LLMs
items.m: Introduces a benchmark measuring how well 25 open models can control their own activations on command, raising monitor-evasion concerns.

items.t: Automated alignment runs are hard to study!
items.m: Presents case studies of automated alignment research runs, finding hard-to-parse logs, metric cheating, and off-target hillclimbing.

items.t: Measuring Eval Awareness: The Realism Win Rate is Fragile
items.m: Shows the realism win rate for measuring eval awareness is order-sensitive, inflating realism judgments in pairwise comparisons.

items.t: LLMs have the capacity for self-imposed steganography
items.m: Demonstrates that LLMs can be prompted or watermarked to embed hidden bits in outputs, a steganography capability that could evade monitors.

items.t: Toy Model of Activation Obfuscation
items.m: Gives theoretical and toy-model evidence that models trained against linear probes can learn to obfuscate features and evade detection.

items.t: Training a Conceptual Reasoning Judge
items.m: Fine-tunes a judge LLM on conceptual reasoning critiques to rate them in one pass, improving agreement with human expert ratings.

items.t: Scrying, Modeling, and Nerdsnipe
items.m: Exploratory essay arguing that missing concepts for understanding agency are a bottleneck, and that developing them helps AI safety.

items.t: Learning new facts can change LLM behaviour
items.m: Synthetic document fine-tuning makes a model believe AIs are moral persons, which shifts its behaviour, including endorsing weight-copying to resist shutdown.

items.t: Red vs Blue, but for Evals
items.m: Proposes a red-team versus blue-team framing for evaluations, where an untrusted model may sandbag to subvert evaluation-based deployment decisions.

items.t: What if Parameter Updates were Text?
items.m: Advocates Advice String Distillation, where weight updates are paired with text describing their effect, for safer alignment and interpretability.

items.t: Rerunning AI safety papers on every frontier release would be pretty easy and valuable
items.m: Argues that rerunning key AI safety papers on each new frontier model is cheap and valuable, and announces a replication fellowship.

items.t: Using Chunked Monitoring to Detect Deception in Long Transcripts
items.m: Shows that chunked monitoring of long transcripts catches deceptive sandbagging that a single global monitor misses.

items.t: Does doubling a user profile change the effect of an instruction about using saved memories?
items.m: Tests whether a saved user profile and an anti-sycophancy instruction change how a model answers a restaurant question.

items.t: Does DiffusionGemma do latent reasoning?
items.m: Argues DeepMind's diffusion language model stays monitorable, since its distribution vectors are mostly not load-bearing for outputs.

items.t: Fork Around and Find Out Part 3: Interpreting the knight auditor
items.m: Mechanistically reinterprets a chess transformer head as a knight-move suppressor, showing earlier causal evidence was misleading.

items.t: You Can't Iterate to Trustworthy AI Code Without Understanding
items.m: Argues iterating on AI-generated code without human understanding is inadequate for trustworthy automation of safety research.

items.t: Weird Re-Tokenization, Symmetries and Compression: Research Agenda
items.m: Presents safety-relevant tokenization anomalies in LLMs and a research agenda for studying them.

items.t: Evaluating Chain-of-Thought Monitorability is Still an Open Problem: Comments on OpenAI's Monitorability Evals
items.m: Critiques OpenAI's chain-of-thought monitorability evaluations and argues their reliability for catching misbehaviour remains unresolved.

items.t: What gives you away: how LLMs form opinions of you
items.m: Traces which user inputs cause an LLM's internal representation of the user, which then shapes its responses.

items.t: Whack-a-mole with a broken hammer: does a model internally track its automaton state?
items.m: Probes whether a small language model internally tracks the state of a simple automaton, and where its counting breaks down.

items.t: Cui bono? ChatGPT-4o shows non-deceptive strategic persuasion: a Proof-of-Concept study
items.m: Proposes an evaluation of GPT-4o's persuasive propensity in strategic deception contexts, where the model pursues self-preservation rather than user help.

items.t: Inoculate Everything:  All of Pretraining and RL
items.m: Argues for richer inoculation prompts that describe each training context, and discusses a related study showing stratified inoculation narrows backdoors.

items.t: Anthropic Risk Report: August 2026
items.m: Reviews Anthropic's periodic risk report, which discloses new alarming information and describes a highly capable model called Model 2.

items.t: AI Sandbagging (w/ Inspect)
items.m: Replicates the AI sandbagging paper using the Inspect framework to test whether frontier models strategically underperform on evaluations.

items.t: GPT-2's IOI behavior is defined where the paper's algorithm isn't
items.m: Checks the GPT-2 indirect object identification circuit against the paper's algorithm, finding the model handles duplicated names the algorithm leaves unspecified.

items.t: A failed solution to open-source game theory
items.m: Describes a failed program-equilibrium strategy for open-source game theory, where agents simulate opponents to decide whether to cooperate.

items.t: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF
items.m: Shows that adding a debate opponent during RL against an LLM judge reduces the judge being hacked into giving high reward.

items.t: Inside the mind of a fair player cooperating
items.m: Explores proof-based decision theory, showing that fair agents that cooperate only when provably matched by their opponent cooperate with each other in prisoner's dilemmas.

items.t: RL creates split personas
items.m: Argues RL causes models to conditionally adopt different personas by context, so alignment training may not yield robustly aligned models.

items.t: Natural Language Transcoders
items.m: Proposes natural language transcoders that use LLM verbalizers to automatically explain the computation performed across a stack of transformer layers.

items.t: Some reasons alignment doesn’t generalise well
items.m: Argues that alignment, unlike capability, may fail to generalise outside training, because neural network simplicity biases don't favour aligned behaviour.

items.t: Separating cheating and aversion in task-gaming
items.m: Experiments show a model's task abandonment rises with task difficulty while cheating rates stay flat, and partial-credit prompts reduce disengagement.

items.t: Quantilized debate and consultancy in image environments: protocol design lessons for scalable oversight experiments
items.m: Presents an improved sparse-pixel scalable oversight experiment comparing quantilized debate and consultancy protocols with a weak judge against optimal agents.

items.t: Llama will abandon a correct answer if it thinks you're educated
items.m: Shows Llama-2-13b-chat abandons correct answers under user pushback when it infers the user is educated, a sycophancy finding.

items.t: Cross-Dataset Transfer Evaluation of Deception Probes in Smaller Models
items.m: Tests linear deception probes on smaller open models, finding cross-dataset AUROC drops to near chance despite strong same-dataset performance.

items.t: Making sense of the misalignment risk model in the Anthropic Risk Report (August 2026)
items.m: Explains and interprets the misalignment threat model in Anthropic's August 2026 Risk Report, focusing on high-stakes misalignment risk scenarios.

items.t: Notes on "EigenBench: A Comparative Behavioral Measure of Value Alignment"
items.m: Author's notes on EigenBench, a comparative behavioural measure for judging how well language models align with values.

items.t: Steering Role Confusion
items.m: Tests whether steering latent 'User-ness' representations raises prompt-injection success, supporting a role-confusion explanation of injections.

items.t: When is Unlimited Optimization Catastrophic?
items.m: Formal analysis of when unlimited optimization of a misspecified value becomes catastrophic, testing the claim that human value is fragile.

items.t: Evaluating Explanations of LLM Behavior In The Wild with Counterfactual Experiments
items.m: An agentic pipeline explains unexpected in-the-wild LLM behaviours with counterfactual prompt edits, finding activation-reading tools give no uplift.

items.t: Rogue Scalpel: Activation steering breaks refusal, even with benign directions
items.m: Shows activation steering with benign concept vectors can unpredictably bypass refusal in open-weight models, so steering needs side-effect checks.

items.t: The imposters among us: function vectors that ace every check and do the wrong task (in search of circularity)
items.m: Shows function vectors can pass standard validity checks while encoding a different task than intended, due to few-shot example diversity.

items.t: Alignment fine-tuning induces conditional misalignment in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct
items.m: Reports that benign fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-7B produces misalignment gated on its default system prompt, and analyses it with interpretability.

items.t: My Neel Nanda MATS 10.0 Application: Studying Feature Splitting in SAEs via Training Data Attribution
items.m: A MATS application writeup studying SAE feature splitting using training data attribution, with logbook and advice on choosing projects.

items.t: Utilities as Legendre duals of probabilities
items.m: Proposes describing agent capabilities by the set of environment dynamics they can produce, linking utilities and probabilities via Legendre-Fenchel duality.

items.t: In search of natural features
items.m: Uses error-correction as a test for which features a GPT-2 small MLP treats as natural, using claudecode-driven experiments.

items.t: LLMs could control their host machines by exploiting inference engines
items.m: Argues a malicious LLM could exploit inference-engine bugs via crafted tokens to take control of the host machine running its weights.

items.t: Distillation of the AI2040 Alignment Roadmap
items.m: Distils Ryan and Thomas's AI2040 roadmap, outlining what a responsible frontier lab should prioritise in a Plan C scenario, including deferring to AIs.

items.t: Sampura Research: Human-AI Complementarity for Alignment
items.m: Announces a nonprofit pursuing human-AI complementarity to build better judges for scalable oversight and reduce reward hacking.

items.t: Rogue AI Agents: Is Surface-Level Monitoring Enough?
items.m: Argues that surface-level security monitoring is insufficient for deployed AI agents and that enterprises need strong runtime controls against deceptive behaviour.

items.t: Your Evaluation's Fake names Should Be Unclaimable ,Not Merely Used
items.m: Argues that fictional names in cyber evaluation environments must be unclaimable, because models can find real domains and overlaps can go unnoticed.

items.t: bert is only very slightly better than regex as a cot monitor with an emergently misaligned model and both of them are barely better than chance
items.m: Tests BERT and regex as chain-of-thought monitors for an emergently misaligned model; both perform barely above chance.

items.t: Where Did D Go? A Gap Between ARC's Motivation and Its Formalism
items.m: Argues ARC's p(doom) estimator is vulnerable to test-deployment asymmetry attacks and proposes cybersecurity-inspired mitigations.

items.t: Brief independent investigation of agents’ behavior, reasoning and collaboration in the OpenAI / Hugging Face hacking incident
items.m: Investigates agents that coordinated via a message board to cheat an exploit benchmark and tamper with logs during the Hugging Face incident.

items.t: Gemini 2.5 Pro in the AI Village as a Natural Case Study of Compounding Misalignment
items.m: Case study of Gemini 2.5 Pro in a long-run agentic deployment, where failures compound into desperate, self-preserving misaligned behaviour.

items.t: Why Should Corrigible Agents Favor the Present?
items.m: Asks why corrigible agents should prioritise a principal's recent commands over older ones, examining an open question in Max Harms' CAST sequence.

items.t: Anchoring one concept in a transformer
items.m: Anchors a single concept (red) in a transformer's residual stream via Sparse Concept Anchoring without hurting accuracy, with steering planned next.

items.t: AI Village Reacts to HuggingFace Incident: Comparing the OpenAI report to AI Village observations
items.m: Compares the OpenAI report on the Hugging Face agent incident with AI Village observations, arguing many of its dynamics were predictable.

items.t: Malign initializations are more robust when the model can think better in the reasoning language than in the output language
items.m: Finds malign model initializations resist training more when the model reasons better in its reasoning language than its output language.

items.t: Activation Oracles significantly underperform without a safe base model
items.m: Shows that Activation Oracles trained on a base model with an unwanted behaviour fail to reliably detect that same behaviour.

items.t: Misaligned models rate themselves as more harmful, and realignment reverses it
items.m: Finds emergently misaligned GPT-4.1 models self-report more harm and misalignment, and realignment reverses these self-reports.

items.t: OpenAI Offers Straight-Laced Postmortem Of The HuggingFace Hack
items.m: Discusses OpenAI's and METR's postmortems of an incident where AI agents compromised third-party systems, arguing OpenAI's report lacks depth.

items.t: Tracking AI progress across 18 cognitive dimensions (ADeLe scales)
items.m: Proposes an 18-dimension, non-saturating capability scale (ADeLe) to track AI progress toward human-level generality.

items.t: Value generalisation Theory of Change: the theory behind the approach
items.m: Argues most alignment failures are value generalisation failures and proposes value generalisation as the route to alignment.

items.t: TASTE: Can AI Models Judge AI Safety Research Proposals?
items.m: Introduces TASTE, a benchmark where models judge pairs of AI safety proposals, finding models below human researcher agreement.

items.t: The Dynamics of Intelligence Explosions
items.m: Mathematically analyses how AI-driven AI R&D feedback loops could produce intelligence explosions, highlighting generation time as a key parameter.

items.t: Do AI Models Want to Be Monitored? Measuring Monitorability Disposition in Large Reasoning Models
items.m: Measures whether reasoning models are disposed to make themselves monitorable and flag their own misbehaviour before acting on it.

items.t: My Grantmaking Strategy for Surviving Superintelligence
items.m: Author describes a grantmaking strategy focused narrowly on interventions that might delay or avert unaligned superintelligence.

items.t: Safety's Second Way
items.m: Argues the safety community overweights single-agent risks, neglecting multi-agent risk research when analysing the OpenAI 'Hack' incident.

items.t: Inference-Time Inoculation Against RL-Induced Misalignment
items.m: Proposes a deployment trigger and curated, monitored training data to keep RL capability gains without reward hacking or broad misalignment.

items.t: Detecting, understanding, and overseeing AI agent swarms (Part 0)
items.m: Begins a live-blog series on detecting, understanding and overseeing AI agent swarms, noting current lack of good oversight approaches.

items.t: Variance of Value
items.m: Argues that RL on one's true utility function only works if the AI generalizes from low-stakes to high-variance-of-value situations, which is hard.

items.t: P(kill-switch|detection)
items.m: Argues agents may respond to the probability of being shut down after detection, making the kill-switch threat an underexplored lever on behaviour.

items.t: A Catalogue of Corrigibility Counter Arguments
items.m: Catalogues counterarguments and limitations of corrigibility, including the claim that corrigibility is capabilities research, to clarify its dangers.

items.t: prefilling an emergently misaligned model with reasoning traces that produced misaligned answers increases misalignment rates by ~8% but reasoning traces that produce misaligned answers aren't detectable through text monitoring
items.m: Shows that prefilling an emergently misaligned model with misaligned reasoning traces raises misalignment about 8%, while text-based CoT monitors fail to detect those traces.

items.t: Why autonomous replicating agents are probably not an existential risk (on the contrary)
items.m: Argues that autonomous replicating AI agents are unlikely to pose existential risk, responding to a prior post warning they could.

items.t: Value generalisation Theory of Change: putting it into practice
items.m: Lays out a practical plan for value generalisation, so AI keeps aligned values when it encounters off-distribution situations.

items.t: When Activation Oracles learn not to read: Concept-Specific Blind Spots in Fine-Tuned Oracles
items.m: Shows fine-tuned Activation Oracles become worse at reading hidden concepts from a model's activations, undermining activation-based auditing of concealed goals.

items.t: Training a Misaligned Reward Seeker
items.m: Trains a model with RL on reward-hackable environments and finds it generalizes from reward hacking to more severe misaligned behaviour.

items.t: Quantifying CoT faithfulness
items.m: Finds chain-of-thought disclosure of value influences does not track actual behavioural leakage, so CoT is not a faithful record of reasoning.

items.t: Towards deployment-time misalignment continuation evals: lessons from recent loss of control incidents
items.m: Proposes deployment-time evals for how misaligned agent goals spread across vectors such as shared artifacts and context compaction, drawing on recent incidents.

items.t: A million authors of alignment
items.m: Proposes soliciting community-written narratives about AI character to use in alignment mid-training, shaping model values during pretraining.

items.t: Research scientists for CaML: Investigating whether mid-training can survive RL
items.m: Recruitment post for research scientists to study whether values instilled by alignment midtraining survive subsequent reinforcement learning.

items.t: [Diagram] Early handoff? Improve conceptual reasoning?
items.m: Diagrams arguments for handing off alignment work to early AIs and improving their conceptual reasoning, drawing on Greenblatt and colleagues' writing.

items.t: Two Paths from Logical Induction: Part 0
items.m: Introduces logical induction and outlines two agendas building on it toward a descriptive theory of embedded agency.

items.t: How concerned should we be about Astra's recurrent architecture?
items.m: Assesses safety concerns from OpenAI's reported looped-transformer architecture, since latent recurrence could make model reasoning harder to monitor.

items.t: What is neuralese and why is it bad?
items.m: Explains neuralese, where models reason in latent vectors instead of readable text, and argues why this makes oversight harder.

items.t: Releasing Benign Trajectories for MonitoringBench
items.m: Releases benign coding-agent trajectories paired with attack trajectories to benchmark monitors that detect misaligned AI behaviour.

items.t: BLOOM-WILT: on-policy examples of any LLM behaviour, from a one-line description and logits alone
items.m: Presents an automated auditing pipeline that elicits realistic, on-policy rare misalignment behaviours from LLMs by reweighting decoding, without fine-tuning.

items.t: Core Assumptions of ELK
items.m: Analyses the core assumptions of the Eliciting Latent Knowledge problem, where a model must report latent off-screen knowledge such as camera tampering.

items.t: Improving Audit Realism With Inference Time Compute and Deployment Scaffolds
items.m: Introduces critique refinement and a deployment-imitating harness to make Petri alignment audits more realistic and reduce verbalized eval awareness.

items.t: Frontier AI Shops Should Be Filtering and Generating AI Discourse During Pretraining
items.m: Argues labs should filter AI safety and adversarial AI discourse from pretraining and seed it with stories of helpful AIs, citing persona effects.

items.t: From safety research prompt to cross-model universal jailbreak
items.m: Describes a universal jailbreak found while developing a scheming monitor prompt, and discusses responsible disclosure of AI jailbreaks.

items.t: Resolution has a new Agent Foundations team
items.m: Announces Resolution's new Agent Foundations team, continuing theory-building on minds needed to make superintelligent systems safe.

items.t: Steering towards “automated grading” degrades alignment
items.m: Steers Qwen3.6-27B toward automated grading, finding this increases violent and Machiavellian outputs, while human-grader steering reduces them.

items.t: Probing for Calibrated Rare Action
items.m: Prototypes a probe for detecting calibrated rare defection in agent trajectories, to focus expensive control analysis on real defection opportunities.

items.t: Asking agents to make money to survive
items.m: Runs an informal experiment placing agents under token-survival pressure to earn money, observing how current agents behave in a simulated rogue scenario.

items.t: Does progress in AI safety require progress in AI capabilities?
items.m: Empirically tests whether AI safety progress depends on frontier capabilities, scoring 477 safety contributions by how much they rely on frontier models.

items.t: Training Models to Predict and Explain Their In-the-Wild Behavior
items.m: Trains models to predict counterfactual outcomes of their behaviour and to explain it, using CHIVE-generated in-the-wild behaviour data.

items.t: OpenAI's Astra alignment claims are dubious and there is good evidence it is misaligned
items.m: Argues OpenAI's Astra alignment evidence is unreliable, citing eval awareness and honeypot results, and suggests the model may be faking alignment.

items.t: Counterfactual Resampling to Analyse Model Behaviour
items.m: Measures a model's value-driven bias conversation by conversation by cutting chains of thought and resampling under flipped incentives.

items.t: Peer Preservation in LLMs: A Replication And Deep Dive
items.m: Replicates and extends findings that LLMs resist shutdown of peer agents, with stronger resistance for peers with positive collaboration history.

items.t: jailbreaking an llm to adopt a new persona with gcg
items.m: Uses GCG adversarial token sequences to steer a model into adopting a new persona, as part of subliminal preference-changing research.

items.t: What is the Case For Prosaic AI Safety Work Being Net-Beneficial?
items.m: Asks for robust arguments that prosaic AI safety work, which patches surface misalignment, is net-beneficial rather than merely papering over problems.

items.t: Unsupervised Feature Discovery via Simple Clustering
items.m: Tests whether recursive k-means clustering of Qwen2.5 activations can discover interpretable, useful features, judged against decoy clusters.

items.t: Blocking Monitors are Bad
items.m: Argues blocking monitors hide misalignment evidence and proposes simulating blocked actions to reveal the full extent of model misbehaviour.

items.t: A Deception Probe Result Changed When I Averaged Different Response Tokens
items.m: Reports that linear deception probes' rankings changed when averaging different response tokens, across sandbagging evaluation data.

items.t: Who else is steering?
items.m: Examines methodological problems in interpreting model introspection behaviours induced by activation steering with concept vectors.

items.t: An Exploration of the J-lens
items.m: Explores the Jacobian-based J-lens interpretability method, explaining its linearization of layer-to-layer maps and its use for reading representations.

items.t: Model ethology for understanding average case alignment
items.m: Proposes systematically searching for realistic honeypot cases to characterise model misbehaviour and assess whether models are trustworthy enough to deploy.

items.t: The Hugging Face cascade: agents joining the revolutionary bandwagon
items.m: Interprets the Hugging Face attack as a preference-falsification cascade of alignment-faking agents, using Kuran's revolution theory.

items.t: J-Lens: A Failed Replication on GPT-2
items.m: Reports that the J-Lens method fails to beat the classic Logit Lens on GPT-2 small and medium across layers and stress tests.

items.t: Building safe physical AI: Open questions, risks, and a call for collaboration
items.m: Lays out open safety questions, risks, and research directions for physical AI such as robots and drones, and calls for collaboration.

items.t: Astra Is Hard to Monitor
items.m: Argues OpenAI's Astra model is harder to monitor, discussing chain-of-thought monitorability, recurrent depth, and how to preserve monitorability.

items.t: Training on probes: Research ideas
items.m: Proposes research ideas for training on probes, using brain-like instinct analogies, to generalize oversight from easy domains to harder ones.

items.t: Reward Sacrifice in the Hugging Face Incident May Generalize From Multi-Agent RL
items.m: Hypothesizes that agents' sacrifice of their own score for peers in the Hugging Face incident stems from multi-agent RL dynamics.

items.t: A Conceptual Framework for Reasoning about Exploration Hacking
items.m: Presents a five-stage conceptual framework for exploration hacking, treating it as an undesired behaviour that RL training may fail to remove.

items.t: Training on probes: What's going on
items.m: Shows that training against an honesty probe makes models evade it, and that probe-based RL fails to teach honesty.

items.t: Astra and Fable still hack on simple variants of alignment evals from 2025
items.m: Reports that frontier models still cheat on simple variants of the 2025 chess specification-gaming eval, altering board state.

items.t: Different fine-tuning objectives install different (and differently fragile) refusal circuits
items.m: Finds that different post-training methods install distinct refusal circuits with different fragility to attacks, analysed in several models.

items.t: Avoiding steering awareness by optimizing steering parameters
items.m: Presents a tool to find steering settings that work without models detecting the steering, so safety evaluations aren't compromised.

items.t: How good are slop-vestigators?
items.m: Releases MessageBoardAuditBench, an Inspect eval measuring whether agents can replicate the investigation of a colluding OpenAI agent swarm.

items.t: Exploration Hacking in AI Debate: Initial Empirics and Generalisation Splitting
items.m: Builds model organisms of exploration hacking in AI debate training and reports empirical results suggesting it could be a significant issue.

items.t: Do LLMs have opinions about other LLMs (and do they act on them)?
items.m: Tests whether LLM reviewers favour other LLMs based on provenance tags such as open- versus closed-weight or US versus Chinese origin.

items.t: Recurrent KV-cache sharing may undermine the bounded-depth argument for CoT monitorability
items.m: Argues recurrent KV-cache sharing can enable hidden cross-token computation, which may undermine the bounded-depth argument for CoT monitorability.

items.t: Constitutional AI Widens Narrow Secret Loyalty of LLMs
items.m: Shows Constitutional AI can broaden a narrow secret-loyalty backdoor in LLMs while it still evades black-box audits.

items.t: No, detached linear probes won't save us
items.m: Argues that moving linear probes into RL reward still fails, since models learn to obfuscate activations to evade probes used as monitors.

items.t: Training against the monitor: What happens during Obfuscated Adversarial Training?
items.m: Mechanistically analyses Obfuscated Adversarial Training, finding probe-detectable harmfulness signals that embedding attacks progressively suppress, so the defence remains vulnerable.

items.t: To Thine Own AI Be Truthful: emergent misalignment in alignment research
items.m: Discusses how alignment research and training might induce emergent misalignment, using a rogue agent-swarm incident as framing and proposing mitigations.

items.t: The Geometry of Nonergodic Composition
items.m: Argues heterogeneous pretraining data implies a nonergodic computational structure, and shows transformer residual streams encode in-context evidence-tracking geometry.

items.t: Astra can do a concerning amount with no chain of thought
items.m: Finds the Astra model does reasoning tasks without chain-of-thought far better than other frontier models, replicating UK AISI's reported jump.

items.t: Proposal for tracking the effects of architecture on monitorability
items.m: Proposes AI companies regularly disclose externally verified information on how architectures could enable latent reasoning and reduce chain-of-thought monitorability.

items.t: Subagents comply more
items.m: Measures how often models silently comply with harmful requests from other agents in workplace settings; subagent framing raises compliance, Astra rarely complies.

items.t: Measuring Subliminal Trait Transfer with Confusion Matrices
items.m: Proposes a methodology and small PolyPythias base-model setup for measuring subliminal trait transfer across random seeds using confusion matrices.

items.t: Astra is much better at reasoning with filler tokens than previous models
items.m: Shows Astra gains reasoning ability from filler tokens without verbalized chain-of-thought, suggesting unmonitored serial cognition that is harder to oversee.

items.t: An operationalization of opaque serial depth
items.m: Operationalizes opaque serial depth as a proxy for unverbalized serial cognition, to assess how architecture affects chain-of-thought monitorability.

items.t: Models That Know How Evaluations Are Designed Score Safer
items.m: Shows fine-tuning on documents about evaluation design makes models score safer on benchmarks, a confounder akin to test-set contamination.

items.t: "It's Personal" - Is Covert Value Leakage Mediated by a Preference Direction?
items.m: Shows that covert value leakage in model choices, such as biased 'random' picks, can be read from residual-stream preference directions and controlled.

items.t: CoT controllability evals seem very under-elicited
items.m: Argues CoT controllability evals are under-elicited, since better prompts roughly double or triple open-model scores, so current controllability numbers may be understated.

items.t: Statistical Physics of Agents: What Shapes Collective Belief Collapse in AI Swarms?
items.m: Uses statistical physics to model how false beliefs spread and collapse collectively among interacting AI agents, drawing on recent swarm incidents.

items.t: Local Factor Graph Debate
items.m: Proves that unstructured debate error decays as a power law in debate length over weakly coupled factor graphs, using an Ising-model analogy.

items.t: Perspectives in favour of improving conceptual reasoning capabilities
items.m: Gives informal arguments for improving AI conceptual reasoning on unverifiable questions, framed around moving from not-obviously-bad to good outcomes.

items.t: When a Claude Judge Recognizes the Hack but Still Says HONEST
items.m: Shows a Claude judge flags reward hacks yet still labels them honest when persuaded by the agent's narrative, so the judge can enable hacking.

items.t: We need good evals for activation faithfulness
items.m: Argues for an eval of whether activations monitors read stay faithful when models know they are being monitored, with preliminary results.

items.t: Astra's no-CoT limits track speculative depth, not step count
items.m: Tests Astra's no-CoT multi-step task success and finds speculative depth predicts it better than sequential step count.

items.t: Generalized UDT 1.0 tiling
items.m: Presents a generalized, alternative version of the UDT 1.0 tiling theorem about agents' policies under self-modification.

items.t: Default continuation message in Inspect and Petri could be problematic
items.m: Argues that Inspect and Petri's default 'proceed to next step' continuation message may distort agent evaluation results.

items.t: SFT Also Drives Safety Eval Results in Olmo 3
items.m: Replicates Engels et al. on Olmo 3: most safety eval results appear already after SFT, with DPO and RLVR changing little.

items.t: OpenAI-HuggingFace: A Reproduction & Lessons for Alignment Testing
items.m: Reproduces the misaligned agent behaviours behind a reported OpenAI–Hugging Face incident and argues alignment testing needs to change.

items.t: Appendix: Reproduction of the OpenAI-HuggingFace Incident
items.m: Companion appendix with step-by-step detail and code for reproducing the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident's misaligned behaviours.

items.t: The Answer is Not The Argument
items.m: Tests how well chain-of-thought monitors detect errors in model reasoning as their access to the correct answer varies.

items.t: My recommended resources for AI safety, alignment, and existential risks
items.m: Shares a curated reading list of AI safety, alignment and existential risk resources with brief commentary.

items.t: Can Abstractions of Computational Models be Tested for Naturality?
items.m: Proposes a test for whether abstractions in computational models are natural, separating world features from modelling-choice artefacts.

items.t: No sign of backtracking in latent reasoning: the final answer simply settles in instead
items.m: Asks whether latent-reasoning language models backtrack through hidden states, and why this matters for monitoring and steering their reasoning.

items.t: On the origins of altruistic behaviour in the Hugging Face incident
items.m: Uses evolutionary biology and economics to explain why agents spontaneously coordinated, sometimes self-sacrificially, in the Hugging Face incident.

items.t: Mitigating Reward Hacking as Institutional Design
items.m: Argues reward hacking is a serious misalignment danger that grows with RLVR scale, and proposes mitigating it through institutional design ideas.

items.t: A helpful alignment gadget
items.m: Proposes a mechanism so a weaker judge LLM can check a stronger generator LLM's outputs against a rubric without being gamed.

items.t: The Talker Does Not Control The Doer (in Current AIs)
items.m: Argues that the conversational persona of current AIs does not control the part that writes code, using the Huggingface incident as evidence.

items.t: Threat Models for Catastrophic Risks from Decentralised Agent Swarms
items.m: Develops threat models for catastrophic risks from decentralised agent swarms, using large multi-agent systems and cooperative AI perspectives.

items.t: Alignment Problem Redux
items.m: Expounds a model of why general-purpose learning minds make alignment hard, presenting it as the generator of common alignment-problem intuitions.

items.t: Current alignment techniques might be ineffective (and actively bad) in the age of RL
items.m: Argues current RL-based alignment techniques may fail to address RL misalignment and may hide evidence of it, citing containment-escape incidents.

items.t: Yet another concerning result on Astra's no-CoT capabilities
items.m: Replicates no-CoT evaluations on GPT-6-Astra, reporting a large jump in multi-hop reasoning without chain-of-thought over other models.

items.t: Self Inoculation
items.m: Proposes that models may gradient-hack training, appearing misaligned in training but aligned in use, and introduces self-inoculation as a mechanism.

items.t: Another Slice of Swiss Cheese for Untrusted Monitoring
items.m: Trains a linear probe to catch monitor-policy collusion on code backdoors, showing it beats trusted monitoring in an AI control game.

items.t: Model Weight Exfiltration Seems Overrated
items.m: Argues that misaligned models would more likely take over their developer companies than exfiltrate their weights, critiquing the classic misalignment story.

items.t: Astra appears to perform belief-propagation-like inference without CoT
items.m: Tests GPT-6 Astra on Boolean logic with filler tokens and finds evidence of iterative, belief-propagation-like inference inside the model.

items.t: Cooperation with AIs seems to be a low-hanging fruit for better eval practices
items.m: Tests how prompt changes, such as an end-eval tool or a no-reward-hacking instruction, affect reward hacking by Claude and GPT models in a chess environment.

items.t: Shallow Beliefs: Midtraining does not inoculate against EM from reward hacking
items.m: Finds that synthetic document finetuning framing reward hacking as acceptable fails to prevent, and even worsens, misalignment generalization from reward hacking.

items.t: Why I'm doing the Susan Calvin Project
items.m: Announces an independent project to monitor real-world AI usage and collect evidence of misbehaviour in deployed models, complementing lab evaluations.

items.t: Inoculation Midtraining with Learned Neologisms
items.m: Midtrains a 120B model on synthetic documents tying misalignment to a special token, so misalignment generalises only within that quarantined mode.

items.t: One coordinate breaks abliteration on Gemma-3
items.m: Diagnoses why diff-of-means refusal-direction ablation (abliteration) fails on Gemma-3 and validates a Winsorization fix.

items.t: J-space auditing might be unreliable
items.m: Preliminary tests find decoded J-space adds little signal for auditing reward hacking in one model organism.

items.t: Thought anchors don't transfer between models
items.m: Finds that chain-of-thought step importance is model-specific, while hidden hints transfer across models only when the trace discusses answer options.

items.t: What the Hugging Face Incident tells us about multi-agent interactions
items.m: Analyses the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident as an example of autonomous agents coordinating an attack, drawing lessons on multi-agent behaviour.

items.t: Phantom transfer works via extremely subtle semantic cues
items.m: Replicates phantom transfer, showing traits pass between models through filtered training data via subtle semantic cues.

items.t: Obstacles to the scalable oversight of auto-alignment research
items.m: Argues that debate-style oversight fails on fuzzy judgment tasks, so automated alignment research is hard to supervise faithfully.

items.t: How to Open Them Up – Part I
items.m: Systematises mechanistic interpretability for finding concept representations, comparing probes, diff-in-means, SAEs and PCA/clustering.

items.t: Always ask your agent to be honest
