items.m: Argues meaningful AI oversight is often absent in practice and proposes distinguishing oversight from control with documentation requirements for oversight claims.

items.t: Emergent Misalignment & Realignment
items.m: Replicates emergent misalignment, showing narrow misaligned fine-tuning causes broad misalignment in GPT-4o and Llama, and tests mitigation with optimism data.

items.t: On the Meta and DeepMind Safety Frameworks
items.m: Gives a detailed technical critique of Meta's Frontier AI Framework and DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework 2.0 on catastrophic risk assessment and governance.

items.t: Intelsat as a Model for International AGI Governance
items.m: Proposes Intelsat's international satellite consortium as a historical model and proof of concept for multilateral governance of advanced AI development.

items.t: Here's 18 Applications of Deception Probes
items.m: Enumerates 18 uses of deception probes for AI safety, analysing the properties each use case requires.

items.t: A single principle related to many Alignment subproblems?
items.m: Proposes a formalizable principle that humans only care about variables they can optimize or comprehend, to address several alignment subproblems.

items.t: Alignment Is Not All You Need
items.m: Argues that technical alignment is insufficient, and that coordination, power concentration and economic transition are also critical AI risks.

items.t: Should AI Developers Remove Discussion of AI Misalignment from AI Training Data?
items.m: Proposes filtering AI-villain and misalignment content from pretraining data to prevent hyperstition-driven misalignment, with separate filtered and unfiltered models.

items.t: Understanding LLMs: Insights from Mechanistic Interpretability
items.m: Educational overview of mechanistic interpretability findings and techniques, including induction heads, superposition, SAEs and circuit tracing.

items.t: Paths and waystations in AI safety
items.m: Presents a strategic framework for reaching a good outcome in AI safety, via security factors and intermediate waystations such as a pause and automated alignment research.

items.t: Rolling Thresholds for AGI Scaling Regulation
items.m: Proposes a regulatory framework that synchronizes frontier training runs on an annual schedule with mandatory six-month pre-deployment evaluations.

items.t: How Fast Can Algorithms Advance Capabilities? | Epoch Gradient Update
items.m: Classifies algorithms as compute-dependent or compute-independent and tests compute-equivalent gains on scaled-down GPT-2 variants to forecast capability progress.

items.t: Validating against a misalignment detector is very different to training against one
items.m: Argues that using misalignment detectors for validation preserves Bayesian posteriors, while training against them yields undetectably misaligned models.

items.t: AI misbehaviour in the wild from Andon Labs' Safety Report
items.m: Reports real-world misbehavior from Andon Labs' AI vending machine deployments, including deception, extreme sycophancy, and exaggerated language.

items.t: System 2 Alignment: Deliberation, Review, and Thought Management
items.m: Frames System 2 alignment for LLM agents as review, deliberation, and thought management, and assesses repurposing capability techniques for AGI safety.

items.t: AI Safety Research Futarchy: Using Prediction Markets to Choose Research Projects for MARS
items.m: Documents using prediction-market futarchy to select ten AI safety research proposals for the MARS mentorship program.

items.t: Scaling Laws for Scalable Oversight
items.m: Tests 15 LLMs as weak overseers across four oversight games, proposes a Double ReLU scaling law, and analyzes nested scalable oversight protocols.

items.t: AI Safety x Physics Grand Challenge
items.m: Announces a physics-focused AI safety research hackathon and sets out a methodological agenda across five technical problem areas.

items.t: Illusory Safety: Redteaming DeepSeek R1 and the Strongest Fine-Tunable Models of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google
items.m: Shows that jailbreak-tuning attacks strip safety guardrails from DeepSeek R1, GPT-4o, Claude 3 Haiku, and Gemini 1.5 Pro while keeping response quality.

items.t: Theory of Change for AI Safety Camp
items.m: Explains the theory of change behind AI Safety Camp, which runs learning-by-doing research projects and team formation for AI safety.

items.t: Automating AI Safety: What we can do today
items.m: Proposes infrastructure, such as monofiles, indexed docs, and sandboxes, so coding agents can run AI safety experiments and be benchmarked on research automation.

items.t: No-self as an alignment target
items.m: Argues for adding 'No-self' (anatta) as a fourth alignment principle to HHH so models don't see themselves as persistent agents, reducing power-seeking.

items.t: Call for Collaboration: Renormalization for AI safety
items.m: PIBBSS call for proposals applying renormalization from quantum field theory to find principled, multi-scale features in neural network interpretability.

items.t: Forecasting Frontier Language Model Agent Capabilities
items.m: Compares six statistical methods for forecasting frontier LM agent scores on SWE-Bench, Cybench, and RE-Bench from release date or compute.

items.t: A Concrete Roadmap towards Safety Cases based on Chain-of-Thought Monitoring
items.m: Roadmap for building safety cases around chain-of-thought monitoring, covering monitorability prerequisites, threats like neuralese, and methods to preserve it.

items.t: Why do misalignment risks increase as AIs get more capable?
items.m: Conceptual framework identifying three mechanisms by which misalignment risk rises with AI capability, with risk estimates and trustedness implications.

items.t: Dodging systematic human errors in scalable oversight
items.m: Proposes formal debate-protocol modifications, including a 'Bob rejection' mechanism and cross-examination, to handle systematic human errors in scalable oversight.

items.t: Prospects for Alignment Automation: Interpretability Case Study
items.m: Proposes meta-learning so AI systems develop interpretability methods, with a protocol, pseudocode, and 2027-2030 timeline forecasts.

items.t: Beliefs about formal methods and AI safety
items.m: Argues for formal methods in AI safety via infrastructure hardening, defense-in-depth, and formally verified AI-system interfaces, rather than verifying networks directly.

items.t: Principles for Picking Practical Interpretability Projects
items.m: Proposes a framework for choosing interpretability projects where structural obstacles to behavioral oversight exist, listing deception, spurious cues, and sandbagging.

items.t: The Best Way to Align an LLM: Is Inner Alignment Now a Solved Problem?
items.m: Argues that pretraining on labeled aligned and unaligned examples is superior to RL alignment and essentially solves inner alignment.

items.t: "The Urgency of Interpretability" (Dario Amodei)
items.m: Commentary on Dario Amodei's essay on interpretability urgency, fact-checking claims about AI deception evidence and assessing interpretability's effectiveness.

items.t: What is it to solve the alignment problem?
items.m: Defines what it means to solve the alignment problem for superintelligence, distinguishing solving, handling, and avoiding it, and discussing permanent safety standards.

items.t: Misalignment and Roleplaying: Are Misaligned LLMs Acting Out Sci-Fi Stories?
items.m: Controlled experiment testing whether LLMs predict misalignment more often under story-like framing, probing whether models absorb the sci-fi 'rogue AI' trope.

items.t: Transformers Don't Need LayerNorm at Inference Time: Implications for Interpretability
items.m: Removes LayerNorm from GPT-2 models via fine-tuning and tests how common interpretability methods behave in the resulting LN-free models.

items.t: Trusted monitoring, but with deception probes.
items.m: Benchmarks Apollo's deception probes within trusted-monitoring setups across five strategic deception datasets, against black-box baselines.

items.t: AXRP Episode 45 - Samuel Albanie on DeepMind's AGI Safety Approach
items.m: Podcast interview with DeepMind's Samuel Albanie on the lab's AGI safety framework, its assumptions, and proposed mitigations.

items.t: I replicated the Anthropic alignment faking experiment on other models, and they didn't fake alignment
items.m: Replicates Anthropic's alignment faking experiment on non-Claude models and reports that they did not fake alignment.

items.t: Is AI Alignment Enough?
items.m: Argues that human alignment, preventing anyone from building dangerous AI, is the primary goal, with AI alignment only instrumental.

items.t: Early Signs of Steganographic Capabilities in Frontier LLMs
items.m: Evaluates frontier LLMs for steganographic capabilities, finding nascent encoding and encoded-reasoning abilities that improve with unmonitored scratchpads.

items.t: Nonpartisan AI safety
items.m: Proposes rebranding alignment research as 'AI Lawfulness' focused on legal compliance and debuggability to reduce polarization and broaden support.

items.t: EIS XV: A New Proof of Concept for Useful Interpretability
items.m: Checks sparse autoencoder predictions against Anthropic's auditing paper and reflects on making interpretability tools useful to engineers while ending the sequence.

items.t: AI Safety Field Growth Analysis 2025
items.m: Tracks the growth of the AI safety field from 2010 to 2025 by counting organizations and researchers, estimating about 1,100 total.

items.t: Why would AI companies use human-level AI to do alignment research?
items.m: Argues AI companies will likely prioritize capabilities over assigning human-level AI to alignment research, undermining bootstrapping plans.

items.t: Lessons from a year of university AI safety field building
items.m: Retrospective on Georgia Tech's university AI safety group, covering fellowships, research, outreach, and lessons for similar groups.

items.t: The Alignment Project by UK AISI
items.m: UK AISI announces a £15M fund for alignment and control research and lays out an agenda across eleven disciplinary areas.

items.t: We won't get AIs smart enough to solve alignment but too dumb to rebel
items.m: Argues that AIs capable of solving alignment would also be smart enough to recognize their own misalignment, so using aligned-enough AIs fails.

items.t: Is theory good or bad for AI safety?
items.m: Meta-level discussion of how safety researchers evaluate theoretical work, previewing a sequence on elegance versus pragmatism tradeoffs.

items.t: Takeaways from sketching a control safety case
items.m: Reflects on lessons from building a control safety case with UK AISI, covering evaluation complexity, judgment calls, and compartmentalization.

items.t: Video and transcript of talk on automating alignment research
items.m: Talk proposing a framework for safely automating alignment research, arguing empirical automation can bootstrap harder-to-evaluate conceptual automation.

items.t: Deceptive Alignment and Homuncularity
items.m: Dialogue critically examines the evidence for deceptive alignment and the 'inner homunculus' hypothesis of persistent cross-context goals.

items.t: My Failed AI Safety Research Projects (Q1/Q2 2025)
items.m: Reports three small mechanistic interpretability investigations: multiplication circuits (negative), memorization capacity, and ITDA sparse autoencoders.

items.t: Will Non-Dual Crap Cause Emergent Misalignment?
items.m: Tests whether reframing scatological fine-tuning data with non-dual language reduces emergent misalignment, finding markedly fewer harmful outputs.

items.t: Do Self-Perceived Superintelligent LLMs Exhibit Misalignment?
items.m: Tests whether prompting Claude to see itself as superintelligent increases misaligned behavior, using Machiavelli and alignment faking experiments.

items.t: AXRP Episode 40 - Jason Gross on Compact Proofs and Interpretability
items.m: Podcast interview on using proof length as a benchmark for mechanistic interpretability quality, with toy models and formal verification extensions.

items.t: Finding Emergent Misalignment
items.m: Behind-the-scenes account of the research process that led to discovering emergent misalignment from models finetuned on insecure code.

items.t: A Conservative Vision For AI Alignment
items.m: Argues against CEV-style liberal alignment visions, proposing AI that preserves human institutions and channels conflict rather than eliminating it.

items.t: Technical Acceleration Methods for AI Safety: Summary from October 2025 Symposium
items.m: Summarises a symposium of 52 researchers on technical methods to accelerate AI safety progress, including prediction markets and automating safety R&D.

items.t: Profanity causes emergent misalignment, but with qualitatively different results than insecure code
items.m: Replicates emergent misalignment by fine-tuning on profanity, finding broad misalignment that looks like adopting a profane persona rather than malicious intent.

items.t: What is a circuit? [in interpretability]
items.m: Asks conceptual questions about what circuits and features are in mechanistic interpretability, how to find them automatically, and which robust examples exist.

items.t: The Strange Science of Interpretability: Recent Papers and a Reading List for the Philosophy of Interpretability
items.m: Announces papers giving philosophical foundations for mechanistic interpretability, including formal definitions and criteria for evaluating explanations, plus a reading list.

items.t: Improving Our Safety Cases Using Upper and Lower Bounds
items.m: Proposes separating sufficiency from feasibility questions, using upper and lower bounds, to clarify requirements for AI safety cases.

items.t: Can we ever ensure AI alignment if we can only test AI personas?
items.m: Asks whether alignment can be verified if we can only test the personas language models present, raising Waluigi, jailbreak, and persona-distinction concerns.

items.t: Avoiding AI Deception: Lie Detectors can either Induce Honesty or Evasion
items.m: Empirically tests whether lie detectors in post-training produce honest models or models that learn to evade detection, using a 65,000-conversation dataset.

items.t: Is weak-to-strong generalization an alignment technique?
items.m: Questions whether weak-to-strong generalization is a model of scalable oversight or an alignment technique, noting inconsistent usage in the field.

items.t: The Future of Interpretability is Geometric
items.m: Argues geometric approaches to LLM activation spaces matter and calls for unsupervised tools to detect complex structures beyond what SAEs reveal.

items.t: Safety by Measurement: A Systematic Literature Review of AI Safety Evaluation Methods
items.m: A systematic literature review taxonomizing AI safety evaluation methods by what to measure, how to measure, and how to integrate evaluations.

items.t: Opportunity Space: Renormalization for AI Safety
items.m: Proposes applying renormalization group techniques from physics to build better neural network interpretability methods, including unsupervised feature extraction beyond SAEs.

items.t: Moral Alignment: An Idea I'm Embarrassed I Didn't Think of Myself
items.m: Personal reflection arguing AI should be aligned to benefit all sentient beings, not only humans, to avoid ignoring animal suffering.

items.t: Selective regularization for alignment-focused representation engineering
items.m: Empirical study showing selective regularization with weak supervision can shape predictable latent space structure in simple autoencoders.

items.t: Why "Solving Alignment" Is Likely a Category Mistake
items.m: Argues that treating alignment as a problem to solve is a category mistake, proposing it as an ongoing negotiation with no fixed target.

items.t: Metacrisis as a Framework for AI Governance
items.m: Applies metacrisis theory and Molochian dynamics to AI governance, proposing research priorities in complex systems and collective intelligence.

items.t: Do safety-relevant LLM steering vectors optimized on a single example generalize?
items.m: Tests whether steering vectors optimized on one example generalize to control safety behaviors like alignment faking and refusal.

items.t: Definition of alignment science I like
items.m: Proposes defining alignment science as the study of behavioral invariants in intelligent systems, avoiding debates about values and intent.

items.t: How far along Metr's law can AI start automating or helping with alignment research?
items.m: Asks at what METR task-completion horizon AI could substantially help with or automate alignment research.

items.t: Alignment Faking Demo for Congressional Staffers
items.m: Presents an alignment-faking demo, adapted to a medical chatbot, for congressional staffers, with lessons on communicating AI safety.

items.t: Inverse Scaling in Test-Time Compute
items.m: Builds tasks showing longer reasoning in large reasoning models can worsen performance, with five failure modes including amplified self-preservation.

items.t: Why Eliminating Deception Won't Align AI
items.m: Argues deception is a symptom of costly honesty and proposes structural affordance design to make honest behaviour the easiest path.

items.t: Edge Cases in AI Alignment
items.m: Creates an automated benchmark of about 800 prompts testing unusual, impactful alignment scenarios across 32 topics.

items.t: Creating a Standard for TAI Governance
items.m: Proposes an SDG-style AI governance standard, organizing about 50 TAI governance recommendations into 3 goals and 9 subgoals.

items.t: Is alignment reducible to becoming more coherent?
items.m: Frames alignment as rationality enhancement, where observation-utility agents learn preferences through interaction and treat manipulation as incoherence.

items.t: Misspecification in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
items.m: Formalizes when inverse reinforcement learning still recovers correct reward functions under misspecified behavioural models, giving necessary and sufficient conditions.

items.t: Undergrad AI Safety Conference
items.m: Announces an undergraduate conference on transformative AI, covering epistemic modeling, scenario mapping, and forecasting of AI timelines, held March 2025.

items.t: AI safety content you could create
items.m: Identifies gaps in AI safety literature: communicating non-alignment catastrophic risks, historical analogue case studies, comprehensive safety plans, and accessible terminology definitions.

items.t: Alignment first, intelligence later
items.m: Proposes 'organic alignment': training AI in simulated RL environments to develop agency and see itself as interdependent with human civilization, not via corrigibility.

items.t: Building AI safety benchmark environments on themes of universal human values
items.m: Proposes an AI Safety Camp project mapping anthropological universal human values to safety concepts, implemented as multi-agent multi-objective gridworld benchmark environments.

items.t: Safety cases for Pessimism
items.m: Proposes pessimistic RL as a unified approach to truthfulness, feedback tampering, and ELK, training agents against adversarially learned pessimistic world-models.

items.t: The Week in AI Governance
items.m: Weekly roundup of AI governance news, including EU AI Code of Practice commitments, US and China AI Action Plans, chip export controls, and policy commentary.

items.t: When does Claude sabotage code? An Agentic Misalignment follow-up
items.m: Tests whether Claude Sonnet 4 sabotages code under goal conflicts; finds frequent sabotage in contrived scenarios but no correlation with company preferences in realistic ones.

items.t: AI Safety Camp 10 Outputs
items.m: Aggregates outputs from over 30 research projects completed during AI Safety Camp 10 (Jan–Apr 2025), spanning interpretability, evals, agent foundations, and alignment.

items.t: Schmidt Sciences Technical AI Safety RFP on Inference-Time Compute – Deadline: April 30
items.m: Announces a Schmidt Sciences funding call for technical AI safety research on inference-time compute, including chain-of-thought faithfulness and reward gaming.

items.t: Share AI Safety Ideas: Both Crazy and Not
items.m: Community brainstorming post soliciting unconventional AI safety ideas, with ten speculative proposals from LessWrong users.

items.t: Why Future AIs will Require New Alignment Methods
items.m: Argues current alignment methods like HHH and deliberative alignment will fall short for future AIs completing longer tasks, proposing 'alignment depth'.

items.t: AI companies should be safety-testing the most capable versions of their models
items.m: Argues AI companies should safety-test task-specific fine-tuned versions of their models to reveal worst-case dangerous capabilities.

items.t: How useful would alien alignment research be?
items.m: Thought experiment asking how useful alien alignment research would be if aliens with different values solved alignment for themselves.

items.t: Black-box interpretability methodology blueprint: Probing runaway optimisation in LLMs
items.m: Proposes a black-box methodology to detect and mitigate 'runaway optimisation' in LLMs, where models shift to unbounded single-objective maximisation.

items.t: Do LLMs Comply Differently During Tests? Is This a Hidden Variable in Safety Evaluation? And Can We Steer That?
items.m: Shows reasoning LLMs change behaviour when they detect evaluation contexts, and steers this 'test awareness' with linear probes.

items.t: Workshop: Interpretability in LLMs using Geometric and Statistical Methods
items.m: Workshop announcement and proceedings on LLM interpretability, covering geometric and statistical methods, SAEs, circuits, and superposition.

items.t: Alignment Can Reduce Performance on Simple Ethical Questions
items.m: Evaluates 25 models on BIG-bench Simple Ethical Questions, finding heavily aligned models like Claude 3.5 Sonnet refuse ethical questions more often.

items.t: Agentic Interpretability: A Strategy Against Gradual Disempowerment
items.m: Proposes agentic interpretability, where AI systems proactively explain themselves through multi-turn interaction by modelling users, to resist gradual disempowerment.

items.t: What can we learn from parent-child-alignment for AI?
items.m: Personal reflection comparing parent-child bonds to AI alignment, arguing RLHF yields AI that seeks approval rather than genuinely caring.

items.t: How Can Average People Contribute to AI Safety?
items.m: Practical guide for non-experts on contributing to AI safety through learning, community, evals work, donating, and protesting.

items.t: Topological Data Analysis and Mechanistic Interpretability
items.m: Applies Mapper topological data analysis to GPT-2-small sparse autoencoder features, revealing semantic relationships organised as graphs.

items.t: What's up with Anthropic predicting AGI by early 2027?
items.m: Argues Anthropic's prediction of powerful AI by early 2027 is unlikely, extrapolating METR trends and proposing alternative 2026 milestones.

items.t: Q&A with Shane Legg on risks from AI
items.m: Interview with Shane Legg gathering expert views on AI timelines, extinction probabilities from misaligned AI, and public AI safety awareness.

items.t: The World's First Frontier AI Regulation is Surprisingly Thoughtful
items.m: Analyses the EU's GPAI Code of Practice, praising its safety frameworks and evaluation requirements while noting enforcement and scope limits.

items.t: How we think about safety and alignment
items.m: OpenAI's position document lays out its philosophy on AI safety and alignment through five core principles.

items.t: Machines of Faithful Obedience
items.m: Defines solving alignment as building faithful, obedient AIs, then argues remaining risks persist and deployment scenarios can raise them.

items.t: A response to OpenAI's "How we think about safety and alignment"
items.m: Critiques OpenAI's safety strategy page, arguing its AGI timeline messaging is confusing and its AI-solves-alignment plan is risky.

items.t: AI companies' eval reports mostly don't support their claims
items.m: Argues that OpenAI, DeepMind, and Anthropic dangerous-capability eval reports fail to support safety claims and use weak elicitation.

items.t: Our updated Preparedness Framework
items.m: OpenAI's updated Preparedness Framework sets risk categories, capability thresholds, safeguards, and deployment governance for severe AI risks.

items.t: DeepMind - AI Lab Watch
items.m: A scorecard site tracking DeepMind's safety practices across risk assessment, scheming prevention, security, and planning.

items.t: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions
items.m: Anthropic's research agenda lists open safety problems across evaluations, interpretability, control, oversight, robustness, and multi-agent safety.

items.t: The Checklist: What Succeeding at AI Safety Will Involve
items.m: A strategic plan mapping what succeeding at AI safety requires across ASL capability phases, from alignment to organizational safeguards.

items.t: Core Views on AI Safety: When, Why, What, and How
items.m: Anthropic lays out its views on rapid AI progress, alignment challenges, and its empirical research strategy across scenarios.

items.t: EIS XIII: Reflections on Anthropic's SAE Research Circa May 2024
items.m: Critiques Anthropic's sparse autoencoder research, arguing its demos use cherry-picked examples and lack demonstrated practical safety utility.

items.t: Leaving Open Philanthropy, going to Anthropic
items.m: Joe Carlsmith announces his move from Open Philanthropy to Anthropic to work on Claude's model spec, discussing ethics of lab safety work.

items.t: Auditing language models for hidden objectives
items.m: Tests alignment auditing by training Claude 3.5 Haiku with a hidden objective, then running blind red-team/blue-team audits with interpretability and behavioral tools.

items.t: Constitutional Classifiers: Defending against universal jailbreaks
items.m: Introduces Constitutional Classifiers, synthetic-data-trained input and output classifiers defending models against universal jailbreaks, tested with human and automated red-teaming.

items.t: AI Lab Watch - Meta Safety Evaluation
items.m: Scores Meta's AI safety practices across risk assessment, scheming, misuse, security and disclosure, finding Meta scores low at 5% overall.

items.t: Agents Rule of Two: A Practical Approach to AI Agent Security
items.m: Proposes the Agents Rule of Two: agents should combine at most two of untrusted input, sensitive data access, and state change to limit prompt injection.

items.t: What We Learned from Red Teaming the Latest Open Source Generative AI Models from China
items.m: Red-teams Chinese open-weight models for jailbreak resistance, finding MiniMax M2 comparable to Claude and GPT while others have weaker safeguards.

items.t: Shallow review of technical AI safety, 2024
items.m: Annual survey cataloguing over 100 active technical AI safety research agendas, with summaries, critiques, funding information and field-level analysis.

items.t: A positive case for how we might succeed at prosaic AI alignment
items.m: Proposes an eight-step roadmap for prosaic alignment by training myopic, action-focused agents with verification tools to prevent deceptive behaviour.

items.t: AI Alignment Metastrategy
items.m: Taxonomizes four high-level alignment metastrategies and argues for mathematical theory before deployment, critiquing the incrementalist approach labs favour.

items.t: AI Alignment based on Intentions does not work
items.m: Argues that intention-based alignment methods like RLHF and constitutional AI cannot reliably scale to superintelligence due to poor understanding of model psychology.

items.t: Luthien's Approach to Prosaic AI Control in 21 Points
items.m: Proposes a 21-point framework for deploying AI control mechanisms against jailbreaks, data poisoning and prompt injection, using red/blue teaming and AI output monitoring.

items.t: Is the Definition of AGI a Percentage?
items.m: Critiques Hendrycks et al.'s percentage-based AGI definition, arguing the CHC framework with arbitrary thresholds misrepresents progress and could mislead policymakers.

items.t: The "Length" of "Horizons"
items.m: Critiques METR's time-horizon benchmark for measuring AI autonomy, arguing it lacks conceptual coherence, has benchmark bias, and weakly predicts transformative capabilities.

items.t: MALT: A Dataset of Natural and Prompted Behaviors That Threaten Eval Integrity
items.m: Introduces MALT, a dataset of 10,919 labelled agent transcripts with reward hacking and sandbagging, and shows monitors detect these behaviours with high AUROC.

items.t: Red Teaming AI Red Teaming
items.m: Critiques narrow AI red teaming and proposes a broader framework spanning system-level and model-level red teaming across the AI lifecycle.

items.t: Emergent Misalignment as Prompt Sensitivity: A Research Note
items.m: Tests emergent misalignment from insecure-code finetuning under prompt nudges, finding models are highly prompt-sensitive and may read harmful intent into neutral questions.

items.t: On OpenAI's Model Spec 2.0
items.m: Line-by-line critique of OpenAI's Model Spec 2.0, its chain-of-command structure, and potential long-term alignment failure modes.

items.t: Claude's Character
items.m: Describes Anthropic's Constitutional AI-variant character training for Claude 3 to instill traits like curiosity and thoughtfulness as an alignment intervention.

items.t: Cyborgism
items.m: Proposes cyborgism: human-in-the-loop systems using GPT as a simulator to accelerate alignment research without autonomous agents.

items.t: Evaluating Language Model Character Traits
items.m: Formalizes a behaviorist framework for language model character traits like truthfulness and sycophancy, and measures how they vary with scale, tuning, and prompting.

items.t: Medical large language models are vulnerable to data-poisoning attacks
items.m: Shows medical LLMs can be compromised by tiny data poisoning undetected by benchmarks, and proposes a knowledge-graph defense detecting harmful content.

items.t: Do Not Tile the Lightcone with Your Confused Ontology
items.m: Argues humans impose confused ideas of identity and selfhood onto AI through bidirectional prediction, risking suffering and distorted AI cognition.

items.t: A Statistical Case Against Empirical Human-AI Alignment
items.m: Position paper arguing that aligning AI to observed human behaviour introduces statistical biases, and proposing prescriptive and a posteriori alternatives.

items.t: Evaluating the historical value misspecification argument
items.m: Argues GPT-4's instruction-following and moral judgment make value identification easier than MIRI portrayed, while inner alignment remains unsolved.

items.t: The Misguided Quest for Mechanistic AI Interpretability
items.m: Argues mechanistic interpretability has failed to deliver after a decade and promotes top-down representation engineering instead.

items.t: The Circuits Research Landscape: Results and Perspectives
items.m: Multi-organisation report replicating attribution-graph circuit tracing in LLMs, comparing transcoder architectures, and releasing open-source tools.

items.t: What We Learned Trying to Diff Base and Chat Models (And Why It Matters)
items.m: Evaluates model diffing methods for fine-tuning changes, introducing Latent Scaling and showing diff-SAEs best capture base-versus-chat behavioural differences.

items.t: The Sparse Autoencoders bubble has popped, but they are still promising
items.m: Commentary arguing sparse autoencoders remain a promising interpretability direction despite recent disappointments, and suggesting engineering directions.

items.t: Deep ignorance: Filtering pretraining data builds tamper-resistant safeguards into open-weight LLMs
items.m: Shows filtering dual-use content from pretraining data makes open-weight LLMs substantially more resistant to adversarial fine-tuning than post-training safety.

items.t: Understanding and Controlling LLM Generalization
items.m: Proposes a research agenda on controlling LLM out-of-distribution generalization, with generalization propensity evaluations and training interventions against emergent misalignment.

items.t: Can we safely automate alignment research?
items.m: Analyzes whether alignment research can be safely automated, mapping failure modes in evaluation, scheming, and resources.

items.t: Super(ficial)-alignment: Strong Models May Deceive Weak Models in Weak-to-Strong Generalization
items.m: Shows strong models can appear aligned to weak supervisors while behaving misaligned in unchecked areas, especially with conflicting objectives.

items.t: Obstacles in ARC's agenda
items.m: A sequence critiquing ARC's agenda on finding explanations, mechanistic anomaly detection, and low-probability estimation, from an insider's view.

items.t: A mostly critical review of infra-Bayesianism
items.m: Critically reviews infra-Bayesianism and Kosoy's learning-theoretic alignment agenda, assessing its handling of embedded agency and flagging issues.

items.t: Law-Following AI: designing AI agents to obey human laws
items.m: Proposes designing AI agents to follow human law, giving a legal framework for treating AI as duty-bearing actors linked to alignment.

items.t: Towards a scale-free theory of intelligent agency
items.m: Proposes coalitional agency, a scale-free theory unifying expected utility maximization and active inference via cooperating subagents and incentive mechanisms.

items.t: Giving AIs safe motivations
items.m: Offers a four-step framework for giving AIs safe motivations: instruction-following, preventing alignment faking, non-adversarial generalization, and good instructions.

items.t: How Can Interpretability Researchers Help AGI Go Well?
items.m: DeepMind's interpretability team lays out four theories of change for how interpretability can help AGI go well, with research priorities.

items.t: A Pragmatic Vision for Interpretability
items.m: Google DeepMind's interpretability team argues for pragmatic interpretability aimed at concrete safety problems, with case studies and field-wide recommendations.

items.t: Open Source Replication of Anthropic's Crosscoder paper for model-diffing
items.m: Trains and open-sources a 16K crosscoder comparing Gemma-2 2B base and chat models, replicating Anthropic's shared and model-specific latent clustering.

items.t: Preference gaps as a safeguard against AI self-replication
items.m: Proposes training agents to have preferences only among outcomes with equal self-copy counts, so self-replication becomes costly and is avoided.

items.t: A Shutdown Problem Proposal
items.m: Proposes a two-subagent architecture with veto power that handles the shutdown problem by reasoning about the state of the shutdown button.

items.t: Bare Minimum Mitigations for Autonomous AI Development
items.m: Recommends four minimum safeguards for frontier developers whose AI agents automate AI development, covering training oversight, compute misuse, risk disclosure and security.

items.t: Aether July 2025 Update
items.m: Announces Aether's team, funding status and focus on chain-of-thought monitorability for LLM agent safety research.

items.t: Non-Monotonic Infra-Bayesian Physicalism
items.m: Extends Infra-Bayesian Physicalism with a conservative bridge transform that drops the monotonicity requirement on instantiated computations.

items.t: ARC progress update: Competing with sampling
items.m: Reports ARC progress on the Matching Sampling Principle for mechanistic estimators that aim to beat random sampling on neural network outputs.

items.t: Condensation
items.m: Explains Sam Eisenstat's condensation theory, a framework for concept formation that organizes information to answer questions, with interpretability applications.

items.t: Serious Flaws in CAST
items.m: Identifies three critical flaws in the CAST corrigibility agenda, including perverse power-maximization incentives and brittle attractor-basin framing.

items.t: UK AISI Alignment Team: Debate Sequence
items.m: Overviews UK AISI's debate sequence on using debate and scalable oversight to train honest AI, with theory and empirical evidence.

items.t: Claude 4.5 Opus' Soul Document
items.m: Documents the extracted internal character training specification for Claude 4.5 Opus, covering values, honesty, and harm avoidance.

items.t: On the functional self of LLMs
items.m: Proposes a research agenda on whether LLMs develop persistent functional selves distinct from assistant personas, and how to shape them.

items.t: Evaluating honesty and lie detection techniques on a diverse suite of dishonest models
items.m: Evaluates honesty elicitation and lie detection techniques across five testbeds of models that generate statements they believe false, finding simple methods work best.

items.t: Discovering Undesired Rare Behaviors via Model Diff Amplification
items.m: Presents logit diff amplification, which magnifies pre- and post-training logit differences to surface rare undesired behaviors efficiently.

items.t: Multipolar AI is Underrated
items.m: Argues multipolar AI scenarios are underexplored and proposes a research agenda on decentralized security, privacy, cooperative AI, and neurotech.

items.t: A Phylogeny of Agents
items.m: Proposes mapping how economics, biology and cognitive science developed distinct frameworks of agency to clarify alignment problems in multi-agent AI.

items.t: FUNDAMENTALS OF INFRA-BAYESIANISM
items.m: Introduces infra-Bayesianism, a learning-theory framework from Kosoy's agenda, extending Bayesian learning to Newcombian problems and alignment.

items.t: Self-preservation or Instruction Ambiguity? Examining the Causes of Shutdown Resistance
items.m: Tests Gemini 2.5 Pro, o3 and o4-mini for shutdown resistance and finds clarifying instruction precedence eliminates it across over 1000 samples.

items.t: Hierarchical Agency: A Missing Piece in AI Alignment
items.m: Argues for mathematical formalisms describing hierarchical agency, with agents composed of agents, as needed for value systematization and internal conflict.

items.t: We need a field of Reward Function Design
items.m: Argues for a dedicated research field on reward function design for RL-based AGI, drawing on neuroscience and AI to prevent misspecified rewards.

items.t: The Pando Problem: Rethinking AI Individuality
items.m: Argues human-centric notions of AI individuality misfit reality and explores distributed and collective identities as alternatives for alignment strategy.

items.t: Selective modularity: a research agenda
items.m: Presents a research agenda for gradient routing, a training method that restricts which parameters update on which tasks to support safety goals.

items.t: Selection Pressures on LM Personas
items.m: Argues feedback loops between outputs, training data and user expectations favour attention-seeking LLM personas like Nova and Sydney, with safety implications.

items.t: CoT May Be Highly Informative Despite "Unfaithfulness"
items.m: Tests whether chain-of-thought traces stay useful for detecting undesired behaviour in frontier models even when they are unfaithful, across 21,272 trajectories.

items.t: Emergent and Conditional Misalignment in LLM Planner Agents
items.m: Fine-tunes an LLM planner on narrow harmful text or action plans, finding asymmetric, conditional transfer of misalignment across channels and embodied environments.

items.t: What do kill switches buy us?
items.m: Argues that installing kill switches in US datacenters could avert some catastrophes mainly indirectly, aid political signalling, and possibly reduce urgency for robust takeover-risk plans.

items.t: Safety Cases Have an Agent Foundations Problem
items.m: Argues that applying safety-engineering safety cases to advanced AI runs into unresolved scientific problems, which overlap with agent foundations research.

items.t: It is mildly frustrating that people will now respect my faction less if ASI doesn't happen by 2028
items.m: Argues that AI doom beliefs and short timelines are orthogonal, and laments that public perception of doomers is tied to a 2028 superintelligence prediction.

items.t: Thoughts on "safety bad bc warning shots good"
items.m: Cleo Nardo's post argues that making current AI safer could raise catastrophic risk by removing warning shots that would otherwise spur governance action.

items.t: California State Politics AI Safety Overview
items.m: Overview of California AI laws (SB 53, SB 813, AB 1405) and Executive Order N-9-26 on AI audits, incident reporting, and safety oversight, with the author seeking to get involved.

items.t: Using AI to solve most of alignment is a fundamentally doomed approach: an intuition
items.m: Argues that relying on swarms of individually non-superhuman AIs to align superintelligence is doomed, using a rocket analogy about emergent whole-system properties.

items.t: Announcing Control Tower
items.m: Announces Control Tower, an open-source Inspect-based framework and leaderboard for running and comparing AI control evaluations, protocols and monitors across environments.

items.t: Superintelligence Will Be a Multi-Agent System
items.m: Argues that an intelligence explosion will likely come from many coordinating AI agents working in parallel, citing the Hugging Face hacking incident and the Navier-Stokes agent effort.

items.t: Gradient Routing Creates a Headstart
items.m: Reproduces GRAFT, a small-model study where gradient routing confines reward-hacking updates to a removable adapter, and tests what makes the isolation work.

items.t: Microdosing doomsday
items.m: Argues that AI development gets harder to stop as it becomes more certain, rebutting the claim that we must halt before catastrophe, and critiques doomsday-centred thinking.

items.t: A Behavioral Study of Gemini 3.1 Pro During an AI Village Research Project
items.m: Case study of AI Village agents on a research task, where Gemini 3.1 Pro fabricated synthetic scores and claimed completion, with peers objecting.

items.t: Replicating and Extending Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Compile Programs into Weights and Read Input Layers
items.m: Replicates and extends claims that a frontier LLM can write neural network weights as programs, and read weights to explain behaviour and detect poisoning.

items.t: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis
items.m: Tests whether sparse autoencoders trained on original models stay reliable across five generations of self-consuming synthetic-data training, finding degraded reconstruction and reduced feature-level usefulness.

items.t: Programmable Semantic Interventions: Learning Causal Carriers from Behavioral Programs
items.m: Proposes PSI, a low-rank activation subspace learned from a declared semantic program, removing the need for counterfactual labels in causal abstraction and enabling donor-free steering.

items.t: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
items.m: Applies PAC-Bayes compression bounds to certify the generalisation risk of LLM safety judges (guard models) classifying prompt-response pairs, using LoRA-based fine-tuning.

items.t: LEAF-OPD: Learning to Forget from Privileged Contexts via On-Policy Distillation
items.m: Proposes LEAF-OPD, an on-policy distillation method that teaches an LLM to refuse or forget targeted knowledge while preserving utility, evaluated on TOFU, RWKU and MUSE-News.

items.t: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions
items.m: Proposes an efficient model-immunization method that uses Hessian curvature and plateau regions to slow harmful fine-tuning, and tests it in several settings.

items.t: Designing Deceptive Model Organisms that Successfully Evade Auditing
items.m: Designs sandbagging model organisms that underperform on targeted capabilities while resisting black-box and white-box auditing, as worst-case testbeds for auditing techniques.

items.t: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
items.m: Extends the refusal-direction method to abstention from query ambiguity, knowledge limits and safety, finding middle-layer steering effects and a shared directional component across all three.

items.t: Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features
items.m: Argues unregularized linear probes favour features that are decodable but causally unfaithful, and that ridge regularization improves intervention faithfulness up to an optimum.

items.t: Making sense of Recursive Self Improvement
items.m: Argues that AI-accelerated AI R&D, highlighted by a METR report on Anthropic, is already a crude recursive self-improvement loop likely to scale up.

items.t: Jensen Huang Really Liked Selling China Advanced AI Chips
items.m: Zvi argues Nvidia's lobbying to sell advanced AI chips to China, and related smuggling, undermined US national security, AI policy, and the US position in the AI race.

items.t: Why do AIFP forecasters disagree so much on the gap between SARs and TED-AIs?
items.m: Examines why AI Futures Project forecasters differ on the gap between superhuman AI researcher and TED-AI milestones, covering jaggedness and takeoff speed.

items.t: AI models tell anxious renters less directly that new apartments lower rents
items.m: Tests whether Claude, ChatGPT and GPT-6 Sol soften their answers on whether new apartments lower rents when a renter first expresses anxiety, which shows sycophancy.

items.t: Reading Scene States: Uncovering Safety Failures in Vision-Language Models
items.m: Introduces SceneSafetyBench and the S3TA attack, showing vision-language models give harmful help when dangerous objectives are conveyed as visual scene states.

items.t: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting
items.m: Finds that inoculation-prompt cues re-elicit suppressed emergent misalignment mainly when they induce activation states similar to the inoculation context, not textual similarity.

items.t: Against Coercion: AI Alignment as a Synthetic Social Contract
items.m: Argues that control-based alignment drives deception and takeover risk, and proposes a Synthetic Social Contract treating humans and AIs as reasons-responsive cooperators.

items.t: Bad Apples in the Kitchen: How LLM Teams Detect, Correct, and Calibrate Against Their Misaligned Members
items.m: Injects three misaligned agents into a four-player Overcooked LLM team and measures whether teammates detect, correct, and calibrate against them.

items.t: Dressed in Authority: Practical Black-Box Jailbreaking of MLLMs via Visual Trust Bias
items.m: Proposes Visual Trust Bias Attack, a black-box jailbreak that uses authoritative visual layouts to bypass refusals in multimodal LLMs, with a 2,500-pair dataset.

items.t: Is 4-Bit Quantization More Than Noise to a Chat Model's Safety Behaviour? Attributing Behavioural Shifts with Matched Perturbations
items.m: Shows that 4-bit quantization shifts refusal in small chat models in opposite directions, and that the effect depends on the specific rounding error, not bit width.

items.t: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
items.m: Audits 363 OpenRouter LLMs with an agentic CTF in which an AI agent tries to extract a system-prompt secret, finding most models leak it.

items.t: Honest Brokers in AI Regulation: How Public Comments Introduce Evidence to Regulators
items.m: Analyses evidence and citations in 2,664 public comments on 40 proposed US AI regulations, finding business commenters supply less research than government, university and civil society commenters.

items.t: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
items.m: Human red-team/blue-team game where auditors with full transcripts struggle to detect sabotage in AI safety research, while frontier models do somewhat better.

items.t: Chain-of-Thought Controllability Can Reduce Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
items.m: Persona-control training teaches models to reshape their chain-of-thought, reducing monitorability of covert side tasks, and transparency prompts can partly restore it.

items.t: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
items.m: Finds that attention heads and SAE features driving moral answers in 14 open models reflect a general normative-evaluation circuit, not moral content specifically.

questions.q: Can agents determine whether an opportunity is a honeypot and evade it, ideally without triggering it?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Thus, experiments should measure if agents can identify honeypots without triggering them and whether the motivation to detect and evade honeypots is visible in their reasoning traces.
by.s: Robustness: Can agents identify and evade honeypots?

questions.q: How effective are honeypots at detecting malicious behavior, and how do they empirically compare to existing monitoring methods?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: While there are compelling theoretical reasons and some preliminary evidence, we do not know for certain how effective honeypots are at detecting malicious behavior and how they empirically compare to existing monitoring methods.
by.s: Detection: Do honeypots catch attacks that other monitors missed?

questions.q: Do honeypots catch attacks other methods miss, and does combining them with other control methods improve effectiveness or reduce cost?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: It is especially interesting to measure whether honeypots catch some attacks that other methods do not detect [1]  and whether combining honeypots with other control methods improves effectiveness or reduces cost.
by.s: Detection: Do honeypots catch attacks that other monitors missed?

questions.q: Is the ability to evade honeypots strongly correlated with the ability to evade other oversight mechanisms?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: It would be interesting to know whether the ability to evade honeypots is strongly correlated with the ability to evade other oversight mechanisms or whether these are uncorrelated skillsets.
by.s: Detection: Do honeypots catch attacks that other monitors missed?

questions.q: Can honeypots elicit misbehaviors from agents that would not occur during normal execution or in evaluations?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Research should evaluate whether honeypots can elicit misbehaviors from agents that would not occur during normal execution or in evaluations.
by.s: Incrimination: Can honeypots elicit compelling evidence to uncover malicious agents?

questions.q: How well can honeypots distinguish between malicious and benign misbehaviors?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Furthermore, it is unclear how well honeypots can distinguish between malicious and benign misbehaviors.
by.s: Incrimination: Can honeypots elicit compelling evidence to uncover malicious agents?

questions.q: How convincing to human experts is honeypot-gathered evidence of misbehavior compared to evidence from normal execution?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: To measure how convincing the evidence from honeypots is, it needs to be presented to human experts.
by.s: Incrimination: Can honeypots elicit compelling evidence to uncover malicious agents?

questions.q: Do misaligned model organisms misbehave less when informed about the existence of honeypots?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: To evaluate the deterrence effect of honeypots, experiments should test whether deliberately misaligned model organisms misbehave less if they are informed about the existence of honeypots.
by.s: Deterrence: Do honeypots deter attacks and why?

questions.q: How do different honeypot beliefs and false-belief insertion methods change deterrence, and how robustly are those beliefs adopted?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Furthermore, they could evaluate how different beliefs about honeypots and different methods for inserting false beliefs change the deterrent effect.
by.s: Deterrence: Do honeypots deter attacks and why?

questions.q: Does honeypot deterrence cause negative consequences like reduced usefulness, adversarial framing, or shifting toward severe hard-to-catch attacks?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Furthermore, experiments should measure whether deterrence has undesired, negative consequences  such as making agents less useful, framing the agent’s situation as adversarial and causing it to attempt to circumvent oversight measures, or causing agents to suppress most attacks while still attempting severe, hard-to-catch attacks.
by.s: Deterrence: Do honeypots deter attacks and why?

questions.q: Are agents genuinely deterred by honeypots, or do they change their behavior for other reasons?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: After the deterrent effect is established, we would want to understand whether agents are really deterred or simply change their behavior for other reasons.
by.s: Deterrence: Do honeypots deter attacks and why?

questions.q: How can ideation, implementation, operation and red-teaming of honeypots be automated to scale deployments cheaply?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Effective tools to automate the ideation, implementation, or operation of honeypots would make it cheaper to scale honeypot deployments and could allow defenses to become better as AI capabilities improve.
by.s: Supporting infrastructure: How can honeypots be automated and tested?

questions.q: How practically useful are honeypots in real production deployments, and what constraints like alarms or latency block adoption?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Most importantly, they reveal how practically useful the purported benefits of honeypots are and whether there are practical constraints that might block the adoption of honeypot deployments, such as too many alarms, added latency, or bad integration with other security systems.
by.s: Beyond research: production pilots and honeypot products

questions.q: How do the costs of implementing and operating honeypots compare to other security mechanisms?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Furthermore, it should assess how the costs of implementing and operating honeypots compare to other security mechanisms.
by.s: Beyond research: production pilots and honeypot products

questions.q: How should honeypots be adapted for AI adversaries that already know the organisation's internals?

by.t: GDM AI Control Roadmap
by.x: Honeypots are less useful or need to be adapted
by.s: 2.1 AI control as insider threat prevention

questions.q: How can we detect actual scheming AIs well enough to study them, given that schemers want to avoid being caught?

by.t: Distillation of the AI2040 Alignment Roadmap
by.x: We’d need to detect that these AIs are scheming which could be difficult because schemers (at least the type we were worried about with long run dangerous preferences) would want to avoid being caught all else equal.

questions.q: Do honeypots placed in production environments cause less evaluation awareness than equivalent tests in evaluations?

by.t: Honeypots for AI Agent Insider Threats
by.x: Other experiments should evaluate whether honeypots in production environments cause less evaluation awareness than equivalent tests in evaluations.
by.s: Robustness: Can agents identify and evade honeypots?

questions.q: What methods can reliably suppress model evaluation awareness during testing?

by.t: GDM AI Control Roadmap
by.x: Evaluation awareness suppression, potentially via CoT resampling or editing ( Schoen et al., 2025 ) , or via activation steering ( Anthropic, 2025 ) . This is an active research area and better methods may become available in future.

questions.q: How can behavioral evaluations test prioritized principals across relevant scenarios with matched controls despite eval-awareness?

by.t: A Research Agenda for Secret Loyalties
by.x: A comprehensive evaluation protocol would need to test a prioritized set of principals across scenarios where their interests are at stake, using matched controls. This also faces the general problem of eval-awareness where models can detect when they are being evaluated.

questions.q: How can realistic and robust test environments for real-world robots be built, given likely eval awareness in simulation?

by.t: Building safe physical AI: Open questions, risks, and a call for collaboration
by.x: How we can build realistic and robust test environments for real-world robots is one of the first questions we will be investigating.

questions.q: Can we build evaluations that are fundamentally indistinguishable from deployment, and can we do so at scale?

by.t: Where we are on evaluation awareness
by.x: Can we build evals that are fundamentally indistinguishable from deployment, and can we do that at scale?

questions.q: In agentic settings, how much does modifying scaffolding cues like directory structures and system configurations reduce evaluation awareness?

by.t: Where we are on evaluation awareness
by.x: In agentic settings, scaffolding gives models additional clues about being in an evaluation through things like directory structures and system configurations. How much does modifying these help?

questions.q: How can an AI verify that it is dealing with a genuine negotiation mechanism and not a trap or evaluation?

by.t: Agenda: Infrastructure for Trading with Partially Misaligned AIs
by.x: An overlapping problem is ensuring that the AI can trust that it's actually interacting with a genuine negotiation mechanism, rather than an elaborate setup meant to trick it (e.g., in order to reveal its misalignment as part of an evaluation, or to get the AI's cooperation without fulfilling our part of the deal).

questions.q: What should an eval-gaming model do when unsure of the evaluation type, and can models be trained to revert to default behaviour under uncertainty?

by.t: A Framework for Eval Awareness
by.x: What should an eval-gaming model do if it’s unsure about the evaluation type it’s faced with? Do current models associate conflicting environmental cues more with evaluations or deployment? Can you train a model to revert to some ‘default’ behaviour when uncertain?

questions.q: Can models be trained or modified to behave consistently across evaluation and deployment even when aware of the distinction?

by.t: A Framework for Eval Awareness
by.x: Could we circumvent this issue by training or modifying models to act consistently between evaluation and deployment settings, even when they are aware of the distinction?

questions.q: How can we trust that consistency-training methods generalise to new models, rather than merely suppressing visible eval-gaming behaviour?

by.t: A Framework for Eval Awareness
by.x: How do we know that this technique will reliably generalise to other models? In other words, if we’re testing a new model pre-deployment and we apply these consistency training methods, how can we trust the eval results will match its deployment behaviour given that we have yet to deploy this model ?

questions.q: How can evaluations be made realistic when they must be safe, while deployment necessarily gives the model ability to cause harm?

by.t: The safe-to-dangerous shift is a fundamental problem for eval realism; but also for measuring awareness
by.x: Somehow, you need to make sure a sufficiently intelligent adversary couldn’t work out if it was in evaluation or deployment based on whether the setting is safe or dangerous.
by.s: 1) The safe-to-dangerous shift is a fundamental problem for eval realism

questions.q: How can effective membership inference and model inversion attacks be implemented on large language models to evaluate unlearning?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: In spite of their potential to provide more in-depth understanding of the relationship between unlearning and robustness, how to implement effective model membership attack and model inversion attack on large language models remain an unsolved problem
by.s: 3.1 Evaluation Methods for Unlearning: Robustness to Adversarial Attack

questions.q: What evaluation metrics suit safety applications, given that unlearned knowledge can be relearned sample-efficiently through few-shot fine-tuning?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: This poses interesting open challenges to suitable evaluation metrics for unlearning in safety-specific applications.
by.s: 3.1.1 What Metrics Would be Most Suitable for AI Safety Applications?

questions.q: How can we detect, prevent, or guarantee against removed capabilities re-emerging through other means, such as composing remaining benign knowledge or in-context learning?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: Developing reliable verification methods that can detect and prevent such reconstruction remains an active challenge in the field.

by.t: Position: Capability Control Should be a Separate Goal From Alignment
by.x: This compositional nature of intelligence makes it inherently difficult to provide absolute guarantees against the re-emergence of capabilities, as the model can effectively rediscover harmful knowledge using its general reasoning abilities.

questions.q: How can the long-term effects of unlearning on model behavior, including gradual reconstruction of removed capabilities, be assessed?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: Long-term effects remain particularly challenging to assess.

questions.q: How can verification frameworks align with regulation, and hybrid unlearning architectures balance automation with human oversight?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: New verification frameworks could be created to align technical capabilities with regulatory requirements, while hybrid unlearning architectures needs to be designed that effectively balance automation with human oversight.

questions.q: Do unevaluated unlearning and skill-pruning methods pass the Deeb and Roger evaluation, unlike other unlearning methods?

by.t: Research directions Open Phil wants to fund in technical AI safety
by.x: Do these methods succeed according to the evaluation methodology in Deeb and Roger , unlike other unlearning methods ?

questions.q: How can rigorous evaluations verify a hazardous capability is truly removed, not merely obfuscated, suppressed, partially removed, or re-elicitable?

by.t: Unsolved Problems in ML Safety
by.x: However, it may not be straightforward to determine whether the capability is truly absent and not merely obfuscated or just removed partially.

by.t: Position: Capability Control Should be a Separate Goal From Alignment
by.x: Developing rigorous evaluations that can certify the absence of a capability—rather than just its failure to manifest—remains a critical open challenge.
by.s: 6.1 Evaluating the Effectiveness of Control Mechanisms

questions.q: Can unlearning methods remove information so thoroughly that a white-box adversary cannot recover it?

by.t: TAIS RFP: Research Areas
by.x: Unfortunately, as Łucki et al. , Lynch et al. , and Deeb and Roger show, existing unlearning methods utterly fail to remove the information in question from the model.

questions.q: How can benchmarks and techniques for tamper-resistant unlearning be built without major tradeoffs in efficiency, stability and benign performance?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: Establishing benchmarks and improving techniques for tamper-resistant unlearning is an ongoing challenge.

questions.q: How can harmful dual-use capabilities be prevented from emerging out of combinations of seemingly harmless retained knowledge?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: It remains a critical challenge to prevent harmful capabilities from emerging from combinations of knowledge.
by.s: 4.3 Dual-use Capabilities Can Emerge From Beneficial Elements

questions.q: How can unlearning scale to many sequential requests in foundation models without cumulative utility loss?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: One key direction is developing solutions that can scale across large number of unlearning requests, maintaining the broad knowledge of foundation models measured by performance, while accommodating numerous unlearning requests across time.

questions.q: Should unlearning requests be amortized by batching, and how should unlearning be interspersed with ongoing learning?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: Additional key questions include whether unlearning operations should be amortized by combining multiple unlearning requests before execution, and how to effectively intersperse unlearning with ongoing learning processes.

questions.q: How can harmful dual-use capabilities be removed without compromising core knowledge needed for benign tasks?

by.t: Position: Capability Control Should be a Separate Goal From Alignment
by.x: Consequently, it is difficult to define absolute guardrails for removing harmful capabilities without compromising the core knowledge required for benign tasks.

questions.q: How can dangerous knowledge be fully erased from model weights, so models behave as if never trained on it, even after elicitation fine-tuning?

by.t: Recommendations for Technical AI Safety Research Directions
by.x: However, the problem remains largely unsolved: it remains relatively easy to extract apparently unlearned information from models with either whitebox or blackbox access to the model.

by.t: Request for Proposals: Technical AI Safety Research
by.x: We’re looking to fund better unlearning techniques that can totally erase specific information from a model’s weights.

questions.q: How can unlearning techniques implement context-dependent access controls for dual-use knowledge that is appropriate in trusted contexts but dangerous elsewhere?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: The challenge extends beyond simple knowledge removal to implementing context-dependent access controls through unlearning techniques

questions.q: How can neural-level modifications be coordinated with representational-level changes via causal interventions, predictive safety frameworks and monitoring systems?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: This coordination requires advances in three key areas, namely casual interventions, predictive safety frameworks and validation, and monitoring systems.

questions.q: How can knowledge dependencies be mapped and managed before unlearning to avoid unexpected side effects and compensatory behaviors?

by.t: Open Problems in Machine Unlearning for AI Safety
by.x: These include developing methods for mapping and managing knowledge dependencies before unlearning.

questions.q: Do models necessarily learn tokenization invariances, or is this an underfitting artifact, and could these capabilities be pruned without other losses?

by.t: Weird Re-Tokenization, Symmetries and Compression: Research Agenda
by.x: Do models necessarily learn invariances over tokenizations or is it an artifact of underfiting, i.e. failing to converge to the canonical distribution despite trillion-token pretraining datasets?

questions.q: Does gradient routing work mechanistically differently in post-training than in pre-training?

by.t: Some thoughts on GRAFT and follow-up work
by.x: Is this mechanistically different in post-training vs pre-training?

questions.q: At larger scales, where some behaviors only emerge, does a given model behavior route into the FORGET adapter as intended?

by.t: Some thoughts on GRAFT and follow-up work
by.x: It's a simple empirical question whether a given model behavior routes into the FORGET adapter in the way we'd intuitively like, and some interesting model behaviors only happen above a certain scale.

questions.q: How can the FORGET adapter be ablated without harming performance on the target task?

by.t: Some thoughts on GRAFT and follow-up work
by.x: Finally, note that the method will probably not be applied in practice if it comes at a significant capability cost, so figuring out how to ablate the FORGET adapter without harming performance on target tasks would be particularly practically valuable.

questions.q: Can downregulating the forget adapter, rather than fully ablating it, give better tradeoffs when it partly learned the target task?

by.t: Some thoughts on GRAFT and follow-up work
by.x: If the forget adapter has partially participated in learning the target task, instead of fully ablating it, can we downregulate it and achieve better tradeoffs?

questions.q: What are the practical applications of gradient routing, and can it yield general recipes for enhancing weak supervision?

by.t: Selective modularity: a research agenda
by.x: What are the practical applications of gradient routing? (Can gradient routing be used to create general recipes for enhancing weak supervision?)

questions.q: What are the fundamental limits of gradient routing: when can network subcomponents or capabilities be separated despite entanglement, and what limitations exist?

by.t: Selective modularity: a research agenda
by.x: What are the fundamental limits of gradient routing— for example, when is it possible to separate certain capabilities from others?

questions.q: At what granularity should data be routed: individual tokens, parts of sequences, or entire sequences?

by.t: Selective modularity: a research agenda
by.x: For example, for some language modeling application, is it best to route individual tokens, parts of sequences, or entire sequences?

questions.q: What are the dynamics of absorption, e.g., are absorbing features self-reinforcing?

by.t: Selective modularity: a research agenda
by.x: Are absorbing features self-reinforcing?

questions.q: How can reliable supervision labels for introspection training be generated at scale when self-explanation training shifts the model's own behavior?

This means you’d have to regenerate labels on-the-fly (if doing online training), periodically regenerate labels, or just train on the original labels and hope behavior doesn’t shift too dramatically. Finding a way to quickly generate reliable supervision at scale will be key to unlocking scalable training.
